items.text: 96 APPENDIX MEDIUM TERM FISCAL PLAN The State Government is required to place a Medium Term Fiscal Plan (MTFP) before the Legislative Assembly along with the Budget in accordance with Section 3(1) of the Tamil Nadu Fiscal Responsibility Act, 2003 (TNFRA). As per Section 3(2) of the said Act, the MTFP shall set forth a multi -year rolli ng target for the prescribed fiscal indicators like Revenue Deficit, Fiscal Deficit and Debt to GSDP ratio, specifying the underlying assumptions made to arrive at those projections. Complying with the said provisions under the Tamil Nadu Fiscal Responsibi lity Act, 2003, a Medium -Term Fiscal Plan for the period from 2026-27 to 2028 -29 is hereby placed before the Legislative Assembly. I.Revenue Receipts The Total Revenue Receipts of the State Government, including the Grants in Aid and Transfers from Union Government are estimated to be Rs.3,50,027 crore in the Revised Budget 97 Estimates 2026 -27 as against the Interim Budget Estimates of Rs.3,44,575 crore i n 2026 -27. The projections for 2027 -28 is estimated to be Rs.3,95,386 crore and for 2028 -29 is Rs.4,46,803 crore, which indicates a growth of 12.95 per cent and 13.00 per cent respectively. The important components are discussed below: 1. State ’s Own Tax Reve nue The State ’s Own Tax Revenue (SOTR) was estimated to be Rs. 2,29,579 crore in the Interim Budget Estimates 2026-27.
items.source: Tamil Nadu Budget Speech 2026-27 (Finance Minister) [Finance department]
items.title: Tamil Nadu Budget Speech 2026-27 (Finance Minister)

items.text: The important components are discussed below: 1. State ’s Own Tax Reve nue The State ’s Own Tax Revenue (SOTR) was estimated to be Rs. 2,29,579 crore in the Interim Budget Estimates 2026-27. It is estimated to decrease to Rs.2,26,740 crore in the Revised Budget Estimates 2026-27. This erosion is not due to any structural weakne ss in the economy but due to administrative decline and systemic leakages across Commercial Taxes, State Excise, Stamps and Registration and Mining. Accordingly, the RBE has seen a decrease of Rs.2839 crore over IBE. Anticipating plugging of leakages in li quor retail vending, mining, registration, revenue augmentation and better administration, the projection of SOTR is Rs.2,58,483 crore in 2027 -28 and Rs.2,94,671 crore in 2028 -29. The growth 98 rates of State ’s Own Tax Revenue are estimated to be 14 per cent in 2027 -28 and 2028 -29. 2. Non-Tax Revenue The State ’s Own Non -Tax Revenue is estimated at Rs.27,835 crore in the Revised Budget Estimates for 2026 -27 which is a marginal increase over the Interim Budget Estimates of Rs.27,704 crore. The State ’s Non -Tax Revenue is projected at Rs.30,062 crore in 2027 -28 and Rs.32,467 crore in 2028 -29, reflecting a growth of 8 per cent annually. 3.
items.source: Tamil Nadu Budget Speech 2026-27 (Finance Minister) [Finance department]

items.text: The State ’s Non -Tax Revenue is projected at Rs.30,062 crore in 2027 -28 and Rs.32,467 crore in 2028 -29, reflecting a growth of 8 per cent annually. 3. This is based on the estimates in the Union Budget 2026 -27. The share in Central Taxes is projected to be Rs.71,285 crore in 2027-28 and Rs.81,265 crore in 2028 -29 by assuming a growth rate of 14 percent annually. 99 4. This has been increased from the estimates in the Interim Budget Estimates 2026 -27 of Rs.24, 762 crore anticipating release from the Union Government for the newly introduced Viksit Bharat -Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Scheme and the arrear grants -in-aid due to be released to Tamil Nadu under the erstwhile Mahatma Gandhi Natio nal Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. For 2027 -28, Rs.35,555 crore and for 2028-29, Grants -in-aid are projected at Rs.38,400 crore, by assuming a growth rate of 8 per cent annually. II.

items.text: For 2027 -28, Rs.35,555 crore and for 2028-29, Grants -in-aid are projected at Rs.38,400 crore, by assuming a growth rate of 8 per cent annually. II. Revenue Expenditure The Revenue expenditure is estimated at Rs.4,05,802 crore in Revised Budget Estimates 2026-27, which shows an increase of 3.19 per cent over Interim Budget Estimates 2026 -27. The Revenue expenditure is projected to be 100 Rs.4,49,319 crore in 2027 -28 and Rs.4 ,97,860 crore in 2028 -29. The important components are discussed below: • The expenditure on account of Salaries is a committed expenditure. In the Revised Budget Estimates 2026 -27, Salaries has been fixed at Rs.91,032 crore as compared to Rs.94,378 crore in the Interim Budget Estimates 2026 -2027. On the basis of anticipated new recruitments, the projected expenditure on Salaries is Rs.1,01,046 crore in the year 2027 -28 and Rs.1,12,161 crore in 2028 -29. • The expenditure on account of committed expenditure on Pensions and Retirement benefits is estimated to be Rs.41,846 crore in the Revised Budget Estimates 2026 -27. Considering the trends in retirement, the expenditure under Pension and Retirement benefits is projected at Rs.46,030 crore in 2027-28 and Rs.50,63 3 crore in 2028 -29. 101 • The Non -wage Operations and Maintenance is estimated to be Rs.19,698 crore in the Revised Budget Estimates 2026-27.

items.text: 101 • The Non -wage Operations and Maintenance is estimated to be Rs.19,698 crore in the Revised Budget Estimates 2026-27. The expenditure under Subsidies and Transfers is projected at Rs.1,91,219 crore in 2027 -28 and Rs.2,09,780 crore i n 2028 -29. • The interest payments for public debt raised in the previous years are a committed liability of the Government and continue to increase every year. The expenditure on account of interest payments is estimated at Rs.78,683 crore in the Revised Bu dget Estimates 2026-27. This expenditure is projected at 102 Rs.89,698 crore in 2027 -28 and Rs.1,02,256 crore in 2028 -29. III.Capital Account In the Revised Budget Estimates 2026 -27, an amount of Rs.56,985 crore is allocated for Capital Expenditure. As the new Government is expected to spend more for capital expenditure, the capital expenditure is projected to be Rs.68,382 crore in 2027-28 and Rs.83,426 crore in 2028 -29. This shows the commitment of the State to constantly improve the allocation for growth -orien ted expenditure while maintaining fiscal discipline.

IV.Revenu e Deficit and Fiscal Deficit The Revenue Deficit in the Revised Budget Estimates for 2026 -27 is estimated at Rs.55,775 crore. On the strength of the revenue augmentation measures, including improved tax 103 administration and collection efficiency, it is expec ted to narrow to Rs.53,933 crore in 2027 -28 and further to Rs.51,058 crore in 2028 -29, thereby creating additional space for capital expenditure in the State. In the Revised Budget Estimates for 2026 -27, the Fiscal Deficit is estimated to be 3.00 per cent of GSDP. In the forthcoming years, Fiscal Deficit to GSDP ratio is projected to be 2.87 per cent in 2027-28. In 2028 -29, it is estimated to be further reduced to 2.80 per cent. The Fiscal Deficit of the Medium Term will be maintained within the targets fixed under Tamil Nadu Fiscal Responsibility Act 2003. V. items.text: The Fiscal Deficit of the Medium Term will be maintained within the targets fixed under Tamil Nadu Fiscal Responsibility Act 2003. V. Public Debt and Liabilities The estimates for receipt and repayment of borrowings have been finalized on the basis of overall borrowing ceiling fixed by the Government of India. The Government plans to a vail a total loan amount of Rs.1,73,445 crore during 2026 -27 and make repayment of Rs.51,971 crore. Liabilities under the Public Account are also reckoned along with the Public Debt. Net increase in Public Debt 104 and Liability is estimated at Rs.1,20,964 cro re in Revised Budget Estimates as compared to the net increase of Rs.1,21,653 crore estimated in Interim Budget 2026 -27. As a result, the outstanding liabilities as on 31 st March 2027 will be Rs.10,98,768 crore, amounting to 27.01 per cent of GSDP in 2026 -27. However, the Public Debt includes an amount of Rs.9,523 crore which should reflect in the accounts of the Union Government after the approval of Chennai Metro Rail Phase – II project as a Central Sector Project. As and when the necessary book adjustments are made by the Government of India, the Public Debt will reduce to that extent. The ratio of Liability to GSDP is expected to ease further to 26.57 per cent in 2027 -28 and 26.10 per cent in 2028 -29. The State thus aims to preserve debt sustain ability as part of its fiscal consolidation roadmap.

items.text: The ratio of Liability to GSDP is expected to ease further to 26.57 per cent in 2027 -28 and 26.10 per cent in 2028 -29. The State thus aims to preserve debt sustain ability as part of its fiscal consolidation roadmap. VI.Guarantees The outstanding guarantees for each year have to be restricted at a level of 100 per cent of the Total Revenue Receipts in the preceding year or 10 per cent of the GSDP, whichever is lower. Th e outstanding guarantees as on 31 st March, 2026 105 were 63.57 per cent of Total Revenue Receipts in the preceding year and 5.04 per cent of GSDP. The outstanding risk weighted guarantees for each year have to be kept at a level of 75 per cent of the Total Re venue Receipts of the preceding year or 7.5 per cent of GSDP, whichever is lower. The outstanding risk weighted guarantees as on 31st March, 2026 stood at 23.46 per cent of Total Revenue Receipts of the preceding year and 1.86 per cent of GSDP. Conclusion While the State Treasury faces inherited debt pressures and administrative shortcomings, this Medium -Term Fiscal Plan charts a decisive, forward -looking roadmap to restore fiscal balance and institutional strength over the next three years. Guid ed by the high -level Revenue Augmentation and Expenditure Reforms Committees, the State is executing a structured framework to systematically eliminate revenue leakages, optimize expenditure, and enhance service delivery. Crucially, this medium -term strate gy not only aligns immediate fiscal 106 consolidation, but also envisages growth to overcome the deficit in the next 2 years with the help of clean, transparent, and better governance.

Driven by deep institutional strength, a vibrant industrial landscape, and exceptional human resources, this strategic roadmap bridges structural repair with enduring economic health —positioning Tamil Nadu as a benchmark for prudent, inclusive, and sustained economic growth. *********

Unlike many states where growth is concentrated in a single metropolitan city, Tamil Nadu has developed a balanced, polycentric urban system anchored by multiple thriving cities that collectively foster regional development. The next phase of urban development must therefore move beyond physical infrastructure to urban transformation—creating cities that are livable, resilient, sustainable, financially empowered, technology-driven and citizen-centric. By embracing innovation, strengthening Municipal institutions and investing in high-quality urban services, Tamil Nadu can position itself as India's model for next-generation urban development and a global benchmark for sustainable urbanization. 5 Policy Direction: Reimagining Urban Tamil Nadu The next generation of urban development in Tamil Nadu must move beyond the traditional approach of constructing infrastructure to delivering measurable improvements in the quality of urban life. The State's urban transformation should be driven by outcome- oriented planning, where every investment creates resilient, inclusive, sustainable and economically vibrant cities. Urban planning must integrate climate resilience, disaster risk reduction and environmental sustainability to prepare cities for future challenges. Basic Grant: A total allocation of Rs.20,054 crore has been recommended. The release of this grant will commence from 2026–27. ULB Performance Grant: A total of Rs.2,507.50 crore has been earmarked as 19 Performance Grant for ULBs. The grant will be released from 2027–28, subject to the ULBs fulfilling the prescribed entry-level and performance conditions. State Performance Grant: A total allocation of Rs.2,507.50 crore has been recommended for the State. Projects worth upto Rs.3,500 crore would be taken up in each Corporation, the share of GoI would be 60% of the project cost and the remaining 40% of the project cost would be contributed by the State Government and the concerned Urban Local Bodies.

items.text: 2.5 Vetri Tamizhagam Vision 2031 Vetri Tamizhagam Vision 2031 for Municipal Administration in Tamil Nadu aims to transform urban local bodies into efficient, sustainable, inclusive and citizen-centric institutions. It focuses on improving basic urban services, strengthening infrastructure, promoting environmental sustainability and ensuring smart governance to enhance the quality of life in cities and towns. 2.5.1 Water Supply  24×7 safe drinking water will be provided in all Corporations and minimum 3 hours daily supply in Municipalities.  Non-Revenue Water (NRW) loss will be reduced below 15% through leak detection, metering and system improvement. 21 20 Urbanization Premium: A one-time Urbanization Premium of Rs.2,000 per person (based on Census 2011 population) is recommended to support the merger of peri-urban villages with adjoining Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) having a population of one lakh or more. The grant is intended to strengthen administrative capacity, improve civic service delivery and upgrade basic infrastructure in the newly merged areas. 2.4 Implementation of the Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Act, 1998 and the Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Rules, 2023 The Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Act, 1998 has been revived and amended suitably by the Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies (Amendment) Act, 2022 (Tamil Nadu Act 35 of 2022). Under the Act, the Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Rules, 2023 have been framed, the said Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Act, 1998 and the Tamil Nadu 21 Urban Local Bodies Rules, 2023 made thereunder have been implemented with effect from 13.04.2023.

It focuses on improving basic urban services, strengthening infrastructure, promoting environmental sustainability and ensuring smart governance to enhance the quality of life in cities and towns. 2.5.1 Water Supply  24×7 safe drinking water will be provided in all Corporations and minimum 3 hours daily supply in Municipalities.  Non-Revenue Water (NRW) loss will be reduced below 15% through leak detection, metering and system improvement. 22 22 2.5.2 Roads  All unpaved urban roads with households will be converted into all-weather paved roads.  Citizen friendly modern Roads-Integrated Road development works will be undertaken with stormwater drains, footpaths, cycle tracks, pedestrian safety and Street lighting to improve urban infrastructure and public convenience. 2.5.3 Street lights  LED streetlights with smart monitoring systems will be installed across all upgraded Municipalities and added areas.  Renewable energy-based streetlights will be promoted for sustainable energy use.

items.text: 2.5.3 Street lights  LED streetlights with smart monitoring systems will be installed across all upgraded Municipalities and added areas.  Renewable energy-based streetlights will be promoted for sustainable energy use. 2.5.4 Urban Greening  One crore trees will be planted across all Urban Local Bodies to enhance urban 23 greenery, improve air quality and strengthen climate resilience.  Undeveloped parks and vacant Open Space Reservation (OSR) lands will be transformed into parks, playgrounds, green spaces and recreational areas.  Sponge parks will be developed to support stormwater management, flood mitigation and groundwater recharge.  Inclusive parks with accessible facilities will be created to ensure equal access and recreation opportunities for persons with disabilities. 2.5.5 Water bodies  All urban water bodies, including lakes, tanks, ponds and reservoirs, will be identified, mapped, protected and safeguarded from encroachments. 24 24  Water bodies will be rejuvenated through desilting, bund strengthening, pollution removal and improvement of inlets and outlets to enhance water storage, groundwater recharge and ecological sustainability. 2.5.6 Sanitation  Cities will be made Open Defecation Free (ODF) with hygienic public toilets.  100% UGSS coverage in all Corporations, including newly added areas, with full household sewer connections.  Mechanized desludging to eliminate manual scavenging.  Treated wastewater will be reused for industry, irrigation and construction purposes.

items.text: 2.6.2 Underground Sewerage Scheme and Faecal Sludge Management 2.6.2.1 Municipal Corporations Out of 24 Municipal Corporations (excluding Greater Chennai Corporation), Underground Sewerage Scheme (UGSS) works have been completed and commissioned for public use in 22 Municipal Corporations. UGSS works have been taken up in Hosur Corporation at an estimated cost of Rs.582.54 crore and the Faecal 37 Sludge Treatment Plant (FSTP) in Sivakasi Corporation has been completed. The Government is committed to extending sewerage facilities to the remaining uncovered areas in all Municipal Corporations. To achieve 100% sewerage coverage in cities where UGSS has already been implemented, additional works have been taken up under AMRUT, AMRUT 2.0, the Smart Cities Mission, Asian Development Bank (ADB)-assisted projects and the KfW-assisted SMIF-TN III programme. These initiatives are aimed at providing sewerage networks to the newly added and previously uncovered areas of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs).

It is proposed to strengthen sustainable solid waste management through the establishment of further Bio-CNG plants, Waste- to-Energy plants, bio-mining projects and the procurement of Solid Waste Management vehicles in Urban Local Bodies during 2026–27.

items.text: 2.7.6 Streetlights A total of 10.56 lakh streetlights are maintained in 24 Municipal Corporations (excluding Chennai Corporation) and 146 55 Municipalities in Tamil Nadu. With a view to reduce electricity consumption in the above- mentioned urban local bodies, 96 percent of these street lights have been converted to LED street lights. Further, to achieve the prescribed standard of one streetlight for every 30 meters in Urban Local Bodies, additional streetlights are being installed at identified locations. Considering factors such as lux levels, wattage categories, road safety requirements, low maintenance costs and environmental benefits and energy-efficient, LED streetlights are being gradually installed across Urban Local Bodies. A statewide enumeration 82 82 and validation exercise has resulted in the identification of 95,077 Core Sanitation Workers across the State. Of these, 77,702 contract and private Core Sanitation Workers have been enrolled in the Tamil Nadu Cleanliness Workers Welfare Board (TNCWWB) portal. PPE kits have been distributed to 5,597 permanent sanitation workers, occupational safety training has been imparted to 256 Sewer Entry Professionals, 66 Duty Supervisors and 4180 desludging personnel and regular health camps are being conducted.

The Mission focuses on 70% annual vaccination of community dogs, sustained and modern ABC infrastructure across all Urban Local Bodies. Intensive mosquito control activities are being carried out to prevent the breeding of mosquito larvae in water-holding containers and to curb the spread of dengue and 89 other mosquito-borne diseases. Source reduction measures, including the elimination of mosquito breeding sites, spraying of insecticides and fogging operations, are being undertaken on a regular basis. To strengthen mosquito control activities, approximately 20,200 temporary mosquito control workers have been engaged in all Municipal Corporations and Municipalities at the rate of one worker for every 300 households, covering about 60,70,631 households. These workers are carrying out intensive anti-larval and vector control measures.

DIRECTORATE OF TOWN PANCHAYATS (DTP) Town Panchayats form the foundation of Tamil Nadu’s transitional urban governance framework, administering emerging settlements that bridge the rural–urban continuum. Constituted under Article 243Q of the Constitution as institutions of urban local self-Government for transitional areas, Tamil Nadu pioneered the Town Panchayat model and became the first State in India to institutionalize this distinct category of urban local body. Town Panchayats facilitate orderly urban growth by extending Municipal services, strengthening civic infrastructure and supporting local economic development before settlements evolve into Municipalities. They play a vital role in promoting balanced regional development and inclusive urbanization, particularly in taluk 127 headquarters, commercial Centres, pilgrimage destinations and industrial towns. Tamil Nadu has 479 Town Panchayats spread across 5,832.33 square kilometers and comprising 7,429 wards. Their combined population, recorded at 66.50 lakh in the 2011 Census, is presently estimated at approximately 76.50 lakh. They therefore constitute a significant segment of the State’s urban landscape. Their primary responsibilities include the provision and maintenance of safe drinking water, sanitation, solid waste management, roads, street lighting and other essential civic services. Through efficient service delivery and sustainable infrastructure development, Town Panchayats seek to improve citizens’ quality of life while fostering clean, healthy, resilient and well-planned urban settlements. 127 126 4. items.text: In accordance with the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, all Town Panchayats have adopted scientific waste management practices, with sustained emphasis on efficient collection, transportation, segregation, processing, resource recovery and responsible disposal. The 479 Town Panchayats collectively generate approximately 1,755 metric tonnes of solid waste per day, comprising 955 metric tonnes of wet waste, 673 metric tonnes of dry waste and 127 metric tonnes of inert waste. The 47 Town Panchayats generating five metric tonnes or more of waste per day have obtained the requisite consent from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board for scientific processing of Municipal solid waste. Door-to-door collection is undertaken predominantly through Battery-Operated Vehicles, supported by scientifically designed route plans to 145 ensure reliable and efficient service delivery. At present, 97 percent of households are covered, with continued efforts towards universal coverage through source segregation, home composting and decentralized waste management. Recyclable dry waste is channeled to authorized recyclers, while suitable non-recyclable waste is transported to cement industries for co- processing. Waste collection, segregation, processing and street sanitation are supported by 17,107 outsourced personnel and 4,720 sanitation workers. During the past five years, infrastructure has been created to process 660 metric tonnes of wet waste and nearly 500 metric tonnes of dry waste per day in 383 Town Panchayats. items.text: 4.7.2 Online Building and Layout Approval System The building and layout approval process has been fully digitized across all 479 Town Panchayats through the Online Building and Layout Approval System. The Board was established with the objective of ensuring planned development, regulation, operation and maintenance of water supply and sewerage services in the Chennai Metropolitan Area. It is also entrusted with the responsibility of protecting public health through the provision of safe water supply and efficient 189 sewerage management and with all matters incidental thereto. Over the years, in addition to its core functions, the Board has adopted information technology–enabled initiatives to improve service delivery. Accordingly, various citizen-centric online services have been introduced to facilitate efficient, transparent and time-bound delivery of services. The Board is headed by a full-time Managing Director, who is responsible for its overall administration. CMWSSB serves an estimated population of approximately 91 lakh across an area of 426 square kilometers within Chennai City. The Board delivers these services through a well- established administrative network comprising 15 Area Offices and 200 Depots. In addition to serving the city, CMWSSB also caters to the water 190 190 supply and sewerage requirements of select urban areas adjoining Chennai, as well as industrial establishments located within its service jurisdiction. items.text: Vision and Strategic Objectives of CMWSSB  The Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) envisions achieving universal, sustainable and efficient water supply and sewerage services across Chennai City. The objectives of the Board are as follows:  Under the initiative " Drinking Water for All," the Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) aims to ensure coverage of safe and clean drinking water supply to all households within Chennai City. Towards this, water supply infrastructure is being extended to the unserved areas of the Greater Chennai 191 Corporation (GCC), thereby ensuring equitable access to protected water for all residents and to progressively reduce Non-Revenue Water (NRW) to below 15 percent through improved monitoring, demand management and operational efficiency.  Elimination of Manual Scavenging : In line with the Government of Tamil Nadu's commitment to eradicate manual scavenging, the Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) has undertaken comprehensive mechanization of the operation and maintenance of the sewerage system.  Skill Training for Sanitation Workers: The Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) implements skill development programme for sanitation 191 190 supply and sewerage requirements of select urban areas adjoining Chennai, as well as industrial establishments located within its service jurisdiction. Vision and Strategic Objectives of CMWSSB  The Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) envisions achieving universal, sustainable and efficient water supply and sewerage services across Chennai City.

The project will ensure adequate and reliable water supply to the residents of the Southern parts of Greater Chennai Corporation, 201 Tambaram Corporation and 20 adjoining Panchayat areas, benefiting a population of 22.67 lakh. (ii) Water supply schemes under progress in added areas Water supply schemes were completed in 40 added areas at a cost of Rs.1375.20 crore. items.text: 5.10.3 Transforming Sanitary Workers into Entrepreneurs Chennai Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (CMWSSB) has taken significant 234 234 initiatives towards the socio-economic empowerment of sanitation workers by promoting entrepreneurship and dignified livelihood opportunities. In this regard, CMWSSB entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DICCI) with the objective of transforming sanitation workers into entrepreneurs. Under this initiative, sanitation workers are enabled to undertake operation and maintenance of sewerage systems for a period of seven years through the use of specially designed Jetting- cum-Grabbing Machines. Priority under the program was extended to 39 legal heirs of deceased sanitary workers, 48 core sanitary workers and 126 individuals belonging to Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) 235 communities from Below Poverty Line (BPL) families, benefiting a total of 213 beneficiaries. To facilitate the procurement of modern sewer-cleaning machinery, a 50% subsidy was provided to the identified beneficiaries under the Annal Ambedkar Business Champions Scheme. An overall financial allocation of Rs.500 crore has been earmarked for the implementation of this scheme. As part of this flagship initiative for the transformation of sanitation workers into entrepreneurs, 100 Jetting-cum-Grabbing Vehicles were distributed to sanitation workers. The initiative aims to provide sustainable self- employment opportunities, enhance the economic independence of sanitation workers and enable them to become successful entrepreneurs. 235 234 initiatives towards the socio-economic empowerment of sanitation workers by promoting entrepreneurship and dignified livelihood opportunities.

TAMIL NADU WATER SUPPLY AND DRAINAGE BOARD (TWAD) Tamil Nadu Water Supply and Drainage Board (TWAD Board) is a statutory organization of the Government of Tamil Nadu established in 1971, specially for the comprehensive development, implementation and stewardship of drinking water supply and sewerage infrastructure across the rural and urban areas of the State, excluding the Chennai Metropolitan Area. With over five decades of public service, TWAD Board occupies a central role in securing safe, adequate and dependable water supply for the people of Tamil Nadu. Its operations encompass the entire spectrum of water management, from source identification and scheme formulation to construction, water quality surveillance and sustained maintenance, underpinned by a well-structured organizational 241 framework spanning the length and breadth of the State. As the nodal bulk water supply agency of the State, TWAD Board taps distant perennial river sources and conveys treated water to rural and urban local bodies through an expansive Combined Water Supply Schemes (CWSS). Upon commissioning, these schemes are operated and maintained by the Board, ensuring continuity of supply in both quantity and quality across all beneficiary areas. Notwithstanding the substantial progress achieved in expanding water supply coverage, demand continues to outpace availability in several regions of the State, necessitating the formulation and implementation of additional schemes. In parallel, TWAD Board also addresses the water requirements of industries and institutions, either through the existing CWSS 241 240 6.

items.text: In parallel, TWAD Board also addresses the water requirements of industries and institutions, either through the existing CWSS 242 242 network or through purpose-built dedicated supply schemes. Sustaining adequate water supply in Tamil Nadu is a major challenge, as the State predominantly relies on monsoon-dependent surface water and groundwater sources, while possessing only limited perennial river resources. Compounding this constraint, a substantial portion of the existing water supply infrastructure is ageing, giving rise to pipeline leakages, transmission losses and service disruptions that affect the reliability and regularity of supply to beneficiaries. To address these challenges, TWAD Board is actively implementing measures to curb Non- Revenue Water (NRW) through the deployment of IoT-enabled smart water meters integrated with a Centralised Water Monitoring System. This advanced digital infrastructure, unprecedented in its scale and scope within the State, marks a 243 decisive transition towards data-driven, precision- oriented water management. Beyond drinking water supply, TWAD Board is implementing Underground Sewerage Schemes in select urban local bodies to meet the growing sanitation demands of expanding towns. The Board is also pioneering the reuse of treated wastewater for industrial purposes, with a dedicated project currently under execution. Concurrently, long-term strategies are being developed to institutionalize treated wastewater recycling at scale, progressively reducing dependence on freshwater sources and reinforcing the commitment of the Government of Tamil Nadu to sustainable water Management. At the field level, four Regional Offices of Chief Engineers are situated at Vellore, Thanjavur, Coimbatore and Madurai. Under these Regional Offices, 16 Circle Offices headed by Superintending Engineers, 85 Divisional Offices 243 242 network or through purpose-built dedicated supply schemes.

Under these Regional Offices, 16 Circle Offices headed by Superintending Engineers, 85 Divisional Offices 244 244 headed by Executive Engineers and 259 Sub- Divisional Offices headed by Assistant Executive Engineers collectively oversee the planning and execution of water supply and sewerage schemes across the State. 6.1 Vision of TWAD Board  Design and implement Combined Water Supply Schemes and Stand-alone Water Supply Schemes using modern technologies to ensure protected drinking water supply to all rural and urban areas of Tamil Nadu within the stipulated timeframe.  Plan, implement and maintain comprehensive Underground Sewerage Schemes within the prescribed timeframe to promote public health and environmental protection in urban areas.  Operate and maintain Combined Water Supply Schemes serving more than one local body and ensure the uninterrupted and 245 systematic supply of drinking water to urban and rural local bodies.  Install smart water meters in all Combined Water Supply Schemes (CWSS) maintained by the TWAD Board and monitor water supply through the Internet of Things (IoT), aiming to reduce Non-Revenue Water losses and ensure the supply of the prescribed quantity of drinking water to local bodies.  Convert treated wastewater from Sewage Treatment Plants into a resource suitable for various reuse applications.  Ensure the long-term sustainability of groundwater and surface water resources through continuous monitoring and effective protection measures. 6.2 Functions of TWAD Board  Plan, design and effectively implement comprehensive drinking water schemes with 245 244 headed by Executive Engineers and 259 Sub- Divisional Offices headed by Assistant Executive Engineers collectively oversee the planning and execution of water supply and sewerage schemes across the State.

items.text: The central share of the rural component, amounting to Rs.2,283.41 crore, has been approved in the State Level Scheme Sanctioning Committee (SLSSC) of the Jal Jeevan Mission on 15.06.2023. These laboratories carry out chemical and bacteriological analysis of water 273 samples, enabling timely corrective action whenever quality deviations are detected. The State Water Testing Laboratory, Chennai, is NABL accredited and recognised by the Government of India as the State Referral Institute. While 32 District laboratories have obtained NABL accreditation, 51 Sub-district and 24 Block-level laboratories have obtained NABL recognition. Accreditation for laboratories in the five newly formed districts is under progress. During 2025–26, 9.43 lakh water samples were tested against a target of 8 lakh with funding from the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and the State Government. During 2026–27, it is proposed to test water samples from all drinking water sources, in combined water supply schemes, schools, Anganwadis and Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs) established under Jal Jeevan Mission. 273 272 6.9 Material Testing and Quality Control Laboratory TWAD Board operates four Material Quality Control Laboratories at Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli and Tindivanam, with the Coimbatore and Madurai laboratories accredited by NABL.

Using Remote Sensing (RS) and GIS technologies, Groundwater Prospects Atlas (HGM) maps are prepared to identify groundwater potential zones and recharge sites. During 2025–26, 400 geophysical surveys were carried out to identify suitable groundwater sources for water supply schemes. 6.11.1 Rainwater Harvesting Awareness In addition to technical initiatives, the TWAD Board actively promotes public awareness on rainwater harvesting. Awareness campaigns and rallies are organized across all districts, supported by LED display vans that travel throughout Tamil Nadu to engage schools, colleges and public spaces. Pamphlets highlighting 275 the importance of rainwater harvesting are also distributed, with a major outreach effort conducted in October 2025. 6.11.2 Proposed GIS Activities for 2026-27 It has been proposed to initiate a transformative project titled "Assets, Utility Mapping and Web Application with Dashboards Using Geo-Spatial Techniques in TWAD Board schemes." This project aims to integrate advanced geospatial technologies into TWAD's operations, thereby enhancing the management of water supply systems throughout Tamil Nadu. By establishing a comprehensive GIS platform, TWAD Board will streamline the monitoring, management and maintenance of its assets, ensuring effective service delivery.

items.text: With a view to fulfilling the aspirations of the citizens, the Government has proposed to execute a mission mode programme namely Chief Minister’s Integrated Urban Development Mission 294 294 (CMIUDM) in the next five years. There are eleven Sub-Missions identified under the CMIUDM covering all the urban area to ensure planned, sustainable and climate resilient urban development in an integrated manner. It is estimated that an amount of about Rs.1.50 lakh crore is required to achieve the mission, of which about Rs.18,000 crore is proposed to be mobilized through external borrowings from World Bank, Asian Development Bank and KfW by TNUIFSL through various options as follows:  Utilization of amount available if any, due to exchange rate variations under the ongoing EAPs.  Additional Financing under the ongoing EAPs.  New line of credits from various External Funding Agencies.  Raising funds from capital market through Municipal bonds. 295 7.4 Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund (WSPF) The Government of Tamil Nadu has created WSPF as a Trust to cater to civic infrastructure needs like water and sanitation in small and medium towns by raising resources from capital markets. This Trust has been created as a not-for- profit entity. The objectives of WSPF are:  To provide financial assistance for setting up infrastructure projects,  To mobilize resources from the capital market under pooled finance structure,  To facilitate the participation of private sector in water and used water sectors through direct investment and public private partnership,  To enable urban local bodies to access debt finance from markets and  To act as the Nodal Agency on behalf of Union and / or State Government for water, 295 294 (CMIUDM) in the next five years.

It is estimated that an amount of about Rs.1.50 lakh crore is required to achieve the mission, of which about Rs.18,000 crore is proposed to be mobilized through external borrowings from World Bank, Asian Development Bank and KfW by TNUIFSL through various options as follows:  Utilization of amount available if any, due to exchange rate variations under the ongoing EAPs.  Additional Financing under the ongoing EAPs.  New line of credits from various External Funding Agencies.  Raising funds from capital market through Municipal bonds. 295 7.4 Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund (WSPF) The Government of Tamil Nadu has created WSPF as a Trust to cater to civic infrastructure needs like water and sanitation in small and medium towns by raising resources from capital markets. This Trust has been created as a not-for- profit entity. The objectives of WSPF are:  To provide financial assistance for setting up infrastructure projects,  To mobilize resources from the capital market under pooled finance structure,  To facilitate the participation of private sector in water and used water sectors through direct investment and public private partnership,  To enable urban local bodies to access debt finance from markets and  To act as the Nodal Agency on behalf of Union and / or State Government for water, 296 296 sanitation and / or any other infrastructure projects. A sum of Rs.302.30 crore has been mobilized through taxable bonds and tax-free bonds by WSPF. Of the above, bonds of Rs.266.30 crore have been redeemed.

items.text: In this direction, the Chennai Rivers Restoration Trust as a Nodal Agency is undertaking various restoration initiatives to improve the ecology of waterways and Waterbodies with the line departments. 298 298 8.1 ONGOING ECO-RESTORATION PROJECTS The Government of Tamil Nadu had accorded administrative sanction of Rs.735.08 crore for the implementation of Integrated Cooum River Eco-Restoration Project (ICRERP) for the stretch from Paruthipattu check dam to the Cooum river mouth in the Bay of Bengal for a length of 32 km. The major restoration components of the project are river channel improvement, interception and diversion of wastewater, solid waste removal, rehabilitation & resettlement, plantation and riverfront development. So far, Rs.613.29 crore has been disbursed to implementing agencies based on the work progress. All restoration works has been completed except Resettlement and Rehabilitation of remaining 773 Project Affected Families located along the Cooum River at 7 locations. CRRT will take steps to resettle and rehabilitate affected 299 families in co-ordination with TNUHDB, GCC and DMA. The ecological restoration of Adyar River from its origin at Adhanur lake to the river mouth for a distance of 42 km was initiated by the Government through administrative sanction of Rs.744.60 crore. The major restoration works being implemented are sewage management, solid waste removal, river channel improvement, rehabilitation & resettlement for project affected families, plantation and riverfront development. Most of the works have been completed by Line Departments concerned except one work being undertaken by CMWSSB, Resettlement and Rehabilitation of remaining 3,236 Project Affected Families at 7 locations.

items.text: The River basins of Chennai are linked with the Cooum, Adyar, Kosasthalaiyar, Palar basins and Buckingham Canal, supporting irrigation, water supply and flood conveyance. CRTCL aims to transform the city's river systems into sustainable, climate-resilient and socially inclusive urban assets. 8.2.2 Proposed Adyar and Cooum River restoration Projects The Government of Tamil Nadu led by the vision of the Honorable Chief Minister will strive with utmost resolve to restore the Cooum and the Adyar rivers to their natural state. Rivers such as the Cheonggyecheon in Seoul of South Korea and the Kallang in Singapore have, through river rejuvenation, become identities spoken of the world over. On similar lines, Global tenders will be invited and a Detailed Project Report will be 303 prepared to transform the Cooum and the Adyar into the very identity of Chennai. River Adyar, originates from Guduvancheri (Chengalpattu District) and flows 43.4 km through Tambaram, Thiruneermalai, Manapakkam, Saidapet, Kotturpuram and Adyar before joining the Bay of Bengal. Similarly, River Cooum Originates from Cooum Tank (Tiruvallur), flows 65 km (including 20 km within Chennai) to the Bay of Bengal. The proposed Adyar and Cooum restoration projects envisage an integrated river restoration and urban transformation programme comprising, inter alia:  Interception, diversion and management of wastewater entering the river.  Water quality improvement measures.  River ecosystem restoration and biodiversity enhancement. 303 302 comprehensive river restoration and urban regeneration initiatives for the waterways of Chennai.

INTRODUCTION 1.1 Mobility as a Necessity and Public Service Good Mobility is a basic requirement for economic activity, social inclusion and human development. In Tamil Nadu, with a population of about 8.53 crore, access to employment, education, healthcare, economic activity and public services depends on the availability of affordable, reliable and widespread transport. For many middle-income households, mobility is directly linked to livelihood security and quality of life. As economic activity is spread across cities, towns, industrial centres and rural areas, accessible and affordable transport is essential for workers, students, patients, farmers and small entrepreneurs. When mobility is 22 inadequate or costly, it affects productivity, education, healthcare access, household finances and the ability of families to save. Public transport must therefore be treated as an essential public good. It provides affordable access to opportunity, in particular for those without private vehicles, including women, students, senior citizens, persons with disabilities and informal workers. It also emphasizes inclusion, safety and balanced regional development.

items.text: Public transport must therefore be treated as an essential public good. It provides affordable access to opportunity, in particular for those without private vehicles, including women, students, senior citizens, persons with disabilities and informal workers. It also emphasizes inclusion, safety and balanced regional development. State Transport Undertakings have provided this vital connectivity for about 2.12 crore passengers every day through its 21,198 buses. However, rising travel demand, and urban expansion mandate further strengthening, modernisation and expansion of public transport through better fleet strength, technology, safety systems and integrated network planning. A strong and citizen-centric mobility system is essential for the State’s 33 economic growth, environmental sustainability and overall quality of life. 1.2 Necessity of Public Transport Public transport is the most equitable and efficient response to rising mobility demand. It enables large passenger movement using limited road space, keeps travel affordable for lower and middle-income households and reduces dependence on personal modes of transport. In State Transport Undertakings remain the backbone of road-based mass mobility, carrying about 2.12 crore passengers every day through an extensive network covering urban, rural, mofussil and inter-State routes. The need for public transport will become increasingly significant with the continued urbanisation of the State. Strengthening public bus transport is therefore indispensable not only for social inclusion and affordable mobility, but also for improving traffic efficiency, supporting sustainable urban growth, 5 protecting the environment and ensuring balanced regional development. 1.3 Necessity of Technology in Modern Bus Transport Technology has become central to the modernization of public transport. In a large and operationally complex bus system, digital tools are essential for route planning, fleet scheduling, crew deployment, preventive maintenance, revenue protection, passenger information and service reliability. Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS), Automatic Realtime Vehicle Location Systems (AVLS), Passenger Information Systems (PIS), electronic ticketing, central control centres, telematics and enterprise resource platforms enable STUs to improve both operational efficiency and passenger experience. Technology also increases transparency, safety and financial discipline. Real-time monitoring helps reduce bunching and missed trips, digital ticketing improves accountability, 66 and data analytics assists decision-making on route rationalisation, fleet deployment and maintenance planning. As Tamil Nadu moves toward electric mobility, gross cost contract operations and integrated urban transport, technology is no longer optional; it is indispensable. 1.4 Tamil Nadu's Vehicle Ecosystem (As on 01.07.2026) Vehicle registration statistics in Tamil Nadu as on 01.07.2026 show an overwhelming dominance of non-transport vehicles.

Their operations cover even the remotest locations, including rural and hilly regions, besides serving uneconomical routes and difficult terrains where transport connectivity is essential. Tamil Nadu State Transport Undertakings are widely recognised for providing reliable, affordable and safe transport services, and have established a strong benchmark in the public transportation sector across India.

items.text: Tamil Nadu State Transport Undertakings are widely recognised for providing reliable, affordable and safe transport services, and have established a strong benchmark in the public transportation sector across India. However, the steady increase in fuel prices, employee salary commitments and interest payments on loans has created substantial financial stress on the STUs, affecting their overall financial sustainability. Even while operating under loss, the STUs continue to deliver essential transport services, keeping in 3434 view the critical need for affordable mobility for both rural and urban population. During the financial year 2025-26 (Unaudited), the STUs collectively recorded a monthly loss of Rs.393.76 crore. Further, the implementation of the 15th wage settlement, along with the increase in Dearness Allowance during 2025-26, has added to the recurring expenditure of the Undertakings. I t i s a l s o n o t e w o r t h y t h a t b u s f a r e s h a v e not been revised since January 2018. This clearly reflects that the primary objective of the public transport sector is to provide service t o t h e p e o p l e r a t h e r t h a n t o o p e r a t e w i t h a profit motive. The State Transport Undertakings continue to provide affordable public transport services to people in both rural and urban areas. items.text: The funds so mobilised are extended as loans to State Transport Undertakings, thereby generating interest income for depositors while also supporting the financial sustainability of the Corporation. The State Transport Undertakings, in turn, benefit through access to working capital loans at competitive interest rates and through simplified and seamless leading procedures. Until 2023, TNTDFC was functioning under the administrative control of the Transport Department. Requests received from the public, school students, elected representatives and local-body representatives, including petitions submitted through the Hon’ble Chief Minister’s Special Cell, were examined by the respective State Transport Undertakings. Key Highlights (As on 01.08.2026):  Public Transport Service Contract: • To bridge the gap between the revenue and expenditure of MTC, a Public Transport Service Contract (PTSC) was signed in 2023 between the Transport Department, G o v e r n m e n t o f T a m i l N a d u , a n d M T C f o r providing Viability Gap Funding (VGF). • Government of Tamil Nadu shall provide Viability Gap Fund for 100% fleet coverage for the financial year 2026–2027.

items.text: 65  Implementation of Electric Buses in MTC (Chennai) Ltd: • To reduce air pollution and promote sustainable urban mobility in Chennai City, MTC has undertaken the initiative to introduce Low-Floor Electric Buses as an eco-friendly public transportation system and thereby contributing towards improved traffic management and environmental sustainability in the city. • 625 E-Buses (225 A/C & 400 Non-A/C) commenced operations from 5 depots viz., Vyasarpadi, Perumbakkam, Poonamallee, Central, and Tondiarpet-1 depots. • In continuation to this 750 Low-Floor Electric Buses (550 AC & 200 Non-AC) will be deployed in 7 depots by two operators under the Gross Cost Contract (GCC) Model in Phase II in the financial year 2026-2027. • To reduce the usage of private vehicles and to cater to the growing population, 6666 o n b e h a l f o f G o v e r n m e n t o f T a m i l N a d u , MTC has planned to introduce an additional 1,000 Low-Floor Air-Conditioned Electric Buses under Gross Cost Contract model as an eco-friendly public transportation initiative.  First and Last Mile Connectivity (FLMC) services to Chennai Metro Rail Limited: • Metropolitan Transport Corporation aims to enhance Metro connectivity, promote eco-friendly public transportation, and ensure seamless urban mobility in Chennai. For this MTC has planned to deploy 220 Air-Conditioned low-floor electric buses under the Gross Cost Contract (GCC) model for providing First and Last Mile Connectivity (FLMC) services to Chennai Metro Rail Limited within an approximate 4 km radius.

At present, 2.45 lakh seats in 4,927 buses are available for online bookings with an average daily booking of 20,930 seats, while the recorded peak was 42,898 seats. Access to OTRS is being widened through additional travel-aggregator integrations. The existing mobile application has been upgraded with more passenger-oriented features and easier navigation. (ii) Automatic Fare Collection System (AFCS) The Automatic Fare Collection System modernises fare collection across the Tamil Nadu State Transport Undertakings by accepting credit and debit cards, QR codes, UPI, NCMC and mobile wallets. It reduces cash handling and revenue leakage, enables real-time transaction monitoring and provides data for operational decisions. Digital tickets presently 104104 constitute 31% of transactions in SETC, 20% in MTC and 10% in the other STUs. The State Bank of India has entered into Memoranda of Understanding with all 8 STUs to provide Electronic Ticketing Machines and software, including operation and maintenance, for 10 years without capital investment by the STUs. The respective STUs are required to provide the necessary depot infrastructure and ticket rolls.

To improve financial sustainability, the STUs need to diversify their revenue sources. With the objective of increasing non-fare revenue from STU buses, a computerised parcel and cargo forwarding service is proposed. The service will cover booking, storage, forwarding, delivery, movement tracking and grievance redressal. Parcels and cargo will be collected, transported in STU buses and delivered to customers. items.text: 5.3 Measures Taken by STUs to Reduce Road Accidents State Transport Undertakings have introduced several proactive measures to reduce road accidents, including the following: • Strict prohibition of mobile phone usage and alcohol consumption while on duty, with stringent penalties for violations. 136136 • Conduct of random breath analyser tests for drivers before commencement of duty. • Surprise inspections by the Police and Transport Department to detect cases of intoxication. • Identification, mapping and rectification of blind spots in coordination with the departments concerned. • Strict disciplinary action against drivers who are repeatedly involved in fatal accidents • Regular training programmes for drivers and conductors, including yoga and meditation to reduce stress. • Upgradation of crew restrooms with modern amenities, including air- conditioning facilities, across 185 locations, while works are in progress in additional 48 depots. 5.4 Accident Involving STU Buses-Statistics The year-wise details of fatal accidents and fatalities involving STU buses are furnished below:- 137136 • Conduct of random breath analyser tests for drivers before commencement of duty. • Surprise inspections by the Police and Transport Department to detect cases of intoxication. • Identification, mapping and rectification of blind spots in coordination with the departments concerned. • Strict disciplinary action against drivers who are repeatedly involved in fatal accidents • Regular training programmes for drivers and conductors, including yoga and meditation to reduce stress. • Upgradation of crew restrooms with modern amenities, including air- conditioning facilities, across 185 locations, while works are in progress in additional 48 depots.

Public transport contributes to these objectives by connecting people to opportunity, while using road space and energy more efficiently than individual motorised travel. items.text: THE INSTITUTE OF ROAD TRANSPORT 9.1 Introduction The Institute of Road Transport (IRT) was established in 1976 at Chennai with the primary objective of undertaking research and training in the transport sector. items.text: The ongoing fleet modernisation programme represents a significant step towards creating a cleaner, safer, accessible and passenger-friendly transport system. Under the programme, 8,390 new buses are planned for procurement, of which 4,785 buses had been 162162 received as on 23.08.2026. The programme includes low-floor buses, electric buses, CNG buses, mini buses, last-mile connectivity buses and non-air-conditioned mofussil buses. items.text: Tamil Nadu’s future public transport strategy will focus on developing a technology- enabled and zero-emission-ready bus transport system. Air-conditioned electric buses, low-floor services, premium electric buses, feeder services and metro rail-linked last-mile connectivity will be progressively expanded, particularly in major urban centres. Gross Cost Contract models may be adopted wherever appropriate to reduce the Government’s upfront capital investment, ensure predictable operating costs, improve fleet availability and maintain professional service standards. 163 Electric buses will remain the immediate priority in the transition towards clean mobility. At the same time, the feasibility of adopting emerging zero-emission technologies, including hydrogen driven buses, may be explored through pilot projects. Their adoption for long- distance, high-capacity and specialised services will depend on technological advancement, safety standards, fuel availability, infrastructure readiness and cost-effectiveness. Digital technology will form the foundation of the next-generation transport system. Real-time vehicle tracking, Automatic Fare Collection Systems, National Common Mobility Card integration, passenger information systems, CCTV surveillance, panic buttons, AI-enabled control centres, predictive maintenance, digital depot management, route analytics, enterprise dashboards and mobile-based passenger services will be progressively strengthened. These measures will improve punctuality, operational reliability, 164164 revenue accountability, maintenance planning and passenger convenience. Passenger safety will remain a non-negotiable priority. Future buses will progressively incorporate Advanced Driver Assistance Systems, collision-warning systems, lane-departure alerts, driver-fatigue monitoring, speed-monitoring devices, camera-based safety systems and enhanced braking assistance.

items.text: This does not require brave resolutions. It requires brave, collective, intelligent work." - Mahatma Gandhi The Government accords the highest priority to rural development and decentralised governance, recognising that the progress of rural areas is fundamental to the State's overall socio -economic growth. With more than half of the State's population residing in rural areas, the Government is implementing an inclusive development strategy that improves infrastructure, livelihoods and public services in every village, carried forward by the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department through the three tiers of the Panchayat Raj Institutions. 4 4 This Policy Note presents a comprehensive policy framework for rural Tamil Nadu under the vision of "Vetri Tamizhagam". The Vetri Tamizhagam Vision Document adopted by the Government envisions villages governed by efficient and transparent Panchayats; served by urban- grade infrastructure, clean water, connectivity and housing for all; and driven forward by empowered women, thriving rural enterprise and assured employment. The programmes of the Department for 2026-27 translate this vision into action. 5 2. Vision 7 7 2. Vision We envision a rural Tamil Nadu where digitally empowered and vibrant local bodies nurture self-reliant and resilient communities; where robust infrastructure and sustainable growth secure an enhanced standard of living; and where rural poverty is fully eradicated and a dignified livelihood is assured for all. Each element of this vision has a concrete meaning in the daily life of the people in rural areas. A digitally empowered village is one where every household can access Government services, entitlements and information without travelling to a block or district office.

items.text: Each element of this vision has a concrete meaning in the daily life of the people in rural areas. A digitally empowered village is one where every household can access Government services, entitlements and information without travelling to a block or district office. A self -reliant village meets its needs from its own resources — raising revenue, maintaining its assets and deciding its local priorities. Robust infrastructure means all -weather roads, assured drinking water, dependable street lighting and sound economic and social 8 8 assets; sustainable growth means development that raises incomes and living standards today without depleting the land, water and natural resources on which the next generation will depend. An enhanced standard of living is felt in everyday life — clean drinking water at the doorstep, a safe and well-lit street, a proper toilet, a pucca house and a village that is clean and dignified to live in. A dignified livelihood is a work that provides not merely an income but security, respect and the confidence to plan for the future — through wage employment, self -employment or enterprise. This vision aligns rural transformation with the Localisation of the Sustainable Development Goals (LSDGs) across the Department's entire portfolio. Livelihoods, housing and women's empowerment build a 9 9 Poverty-free village with enhanced livelihoods, a Socially just and socially secured village and a Women- friendly village, advancing No Poverty (SDG 1), Zero Hunger (SDG 2), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 8) and Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10).

items.title: Tamil Nadu Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department: Policy Note 2026-27

items.text: Drinking water, sanitation and waste management build a Water -sufficient village, a clean and green village and a Healthy village, advancing Clean Water and Sanitation (SDG 6) and Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3), while the protection of water bodies from untreated discharge safeguards Life Below Water (SDG 14). Roads, community assets, renewable energy and digital connectivity build a Village with self -sufficient infrastructure, advancing Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 7), Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9), Sustainable Cities 10 10 and Communities (SDG 11), Responsible Consumption and Production (SDG 12) and Climate Action (SDG 13). Transparent, participatory and accountable Panchayats build a Village with good governance, advancing Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions (SDG 16) and Partnerships for the Goals (SDG 17). The policy framework rests on three Pillars — Poverty Alleviation, Improving Quality of Life and Strengthening Governance — under which the entire programme of the Department for 202 6-27 is organised. The First Pillar, Poverty Alleviation , ensures dignified livelihoods for all rural households, expands affordable housing and promotes the economic and social empowerment of women through Self -Help Groups, entrepreneurship and financial 11 11 inclusion.

items.text: The First Pillar, Poverty Alleviation , ensures dignified livelihoods for all rural households, expands affordable housing and promotes the economic and social empowerment of women through Self -Help Groups, entrepreneurship and financial 11 11 inclusion. The Government has adopted a comprehensive approach encompassing guaranteed wage employment under VB - GRAM, quality housing for every eligible family under Vetri Veedu Thittam with modern construction technologies and adequate plinth area, and the strengthening of the Self -Help Group movement — through initiatives such as the Singappenngal Valimaippaduthum Thittam — as the prime vehicle for rural women's access to credit, income -generating activities, leadership and participation in local governance. Special focus is placed on women, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups, with universal access to drinking water and household toilets completing the foundation of a dignified life. 12 12 The Second Pillar, Improving Quality of Life, creates resilient public infrastructure and raises living standards through climate - resilient and environmentally sustainable development. Its centrepiece is TN -VETRI, the integrated development initiative of the Department, under which the infrastructure of every Village Panchayat — drinking water, sanitation, rural connectivity, community assets, and the special needs of Hilly and Peri -Urban Panchayats — is assessed as a whole and developed through need-based, gap- based and ge ography- based planning, in alignment with the Central schemes implemented in the State. Roads, Educational Institutions, Anganwadi centres, community halls and other public assets, together with effective waste management and sanitation, are being strengthened to improve public health, dignity and environmental sustainability.

items.title: Tamil Nadu Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department: Policy Note 2026-27

items.text: Roads, Educational Institutions, Anganwadi centres, community halls and other public assets, together with effective waste management and sanitation, are being strengthened to improve public health, dignity and environmental sustainability. 13 13 The Third Pillar, Strengthening Governance, prioritises the digital transformation of Rural Local Bodies, institutional capacity building, sound financial management and citizen participation, so that Village Panchayats become self-reliant, resilient and capable of responding to future developmental challenges. Capacity building of elected representatives and functionaries, participatory village development planning, strengthened own- source revenue, digital service delivery, timely grievance redressal and social audit together underpin transparent and accountable local government. Through these three Pillars, the Department is pursuing medium- term and long-term strategies for resilient, financially empowered, environmentally sustainable 14 14 and citizen -centric Rural Local Bodies. Digital governance initiatives are improving administrative efficiency, transparency, monitoring and citizen service delivery, while sustainability is integrated into rural development through water conservation, renewable energy, natural resource management and climate -resilient infrastructure. The Department remains committed to building resilient, self -reliant and prosperous rural communities, ensuring an improved quality of life and sustainable development for all. Progress under this vision is measured. The Panchayat Advancement Index (PAI), the national framework of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, assesses the development and performance of every Gram Panchayat against the Localisation of the Sustainable Development Goals; the 15 15 State Government is further developing its own expanded Panchayat Development Index (PDI) to capture the priorities of Tamil Nadu's villages.

items.text: The Change Strategy depicted below shows how the Vetri Tamizhagam vision flows through the three Pillars of Change and their building blocks into the village outcomes of the LSDGs — the chain along which this Policy Note is organised and progress will be measured. 16 16 This Policy Note accordingly presents an overview of the State's rural profile, the governance architecture and institutional arrangements of the Panchayat Raj Institutions, their financial framework, developmental achievements and the key challenges confronting Rural Local Bodies, and then sets out, Pillar by Pillar, the policy interventions and programmes proposed for 2026-27 — towards administrative efficiency, better public service delivery, sustainable management of rural assets, stronger local democracy, digital transformation and accelerated, inclusive rural development. 17 3. Panchayat Raj - Overview 19 19 3. Panchayat Raj – Overview The Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) in Tamil Nadu derive their constitutional authority from Part IX of the Constitution of India (A rticles 243 to 243 -O), inserted by the 73 rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which came into force on 24 th April 1993. The State has implemented these provisions through the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Act, 1994. The Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department plays a central role in advancing this vision by strengthening rural infrastructure, enhancing service delivery, promoting sustainable livelihoods, and empowering Panchayat Raj Institutions. The three-tier Panchayat Raj system comprising Village Panc hayats, Panchayat Unions, and District Panchayats serves as the foundation of grassroots democracy, ensuring 20 20 participatory planning and effective local governance through Gram Sabhas and other community-based institutions.

items.text: The three-tier Panchayat Raj system comprising Village Panc hayats, Panchayat Unions, and District Panchayats serves as the foundation of grassroots democracy, ensuring 20 20 participatory planning and effective local governance through Gram Sabhas and other community-based institutions. In line with the Seventy -third Constitutional Amendment, the Government aims to strengthen Panchayat Raj Institutions through the devolution of functions, funds, and functionaries, while promoting transparency, accountability, capacity building and sound financial management. Community participation, habitation-level planning, and convergence of development programmes are emphasised to ensure equitable and need- based development. 21 21 3.1. The Department is headed by the Hon'ble Minister for Rural Development, who provides overall policy direction, while the Secretary to Government is responsible for policy form ulation, legislative matters, administrative oversight, financial planning, and coordination with various Government Departments. The Commissioner of Rural 24 24 Development and Panchayat Raj functions as the Head of the Department and is entrusted with the implementation of Government policies, administration of rural development programmes, strengthening of Panchayat Raj Institutions, monitoring of Rural Local Bodies, and overall supervision of departmental activities throughout the State. The Commissioner of Rural Development (Training) is responsible for capacity building and professional development of Government officials and elected representatives through structured training programmes. The Tamil Nadu State Election Commission is constitutionally mandated to conduct free and fair elections to Rural and Urban Local Bodies, while the Tamil Nadu Delimitation Commission undertakes delimitation of territorial constituencies and 25 25 fixation of ward boundaries to ensure equitable representation in accordance with statutory provisions. Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department has separate gazetted officers in the cadre of Additional Director, Joint Director and Assistant Director cadre who are governed by Tamil Nadu Panchayat Development Service Rules. Block Development Officers are governed by Tamil Nadu Panchayat Development Subordinate Service rule. At the district level, the District Collector functions as the Inspector of Panchayats and exercises overall supervision and control over Rural Local Bodies wi thin the district. Moreover, District Collector serves as the principal coordinating institution for rural development programmes, assisted by the Project Director, Executive Engineer, 26 26 Assistant Project Officers. The Project Director, District Rural Development Agency (DRDA), is responsible for planning, coordinating, implementing, and monitoring major rural development programmes and flagship schemes.

items.text: The Project Director, District Rural Development Agency (DRDA), is responsible for planning, coordinating, implementing, and monitoring major rural development programmes and flagship schemes. The Assistant Directors (Panchayats & Audit) oversee Panchayat administration, statutory compliance, and institutional governance, ensure financial discipline, audit compliance, and accountability in Rural Local Bodies. Assistant Executive Engineers having the responsibility of technical supervision in the technical subdivisions comprise of blocks. At the block level, the Block Development Officers supervise the implementation of Government schemes, provide technical guidance to Village Panchayats, coordinate developmental activities, and monitor programme 27 27 performance, he is assisted by technical officers- Assistant Engineers/Block Engineers, Overseers and Road Inspectors. At the Village Panchayat level, Panchayat Secretaries, Village -level functionaries, technical personnel, and other field staff assist the elected Village Panchayats in maintaining statutory records, implementing development works, managing local finances, delivering essential public services, and ensuring compliance with the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Act, 1994, and the rules framed thereunder. They also serve as the primary interface between the Government and rural communities, facilitating citizen participation and effective grassroots governance. 28 28 Institutional support for strengthening local governance is provided through the State Institute of Rural Development (SIRD) and the Regional Institutes of Rural Development (RIRDs), which organise induction training, refresher courses, thematic workshops, research activities, and capacity-building programmes for Government officials, elected representatives, and other stakeholders. 3.3. items.text: 3.3. Panchayat Raj Institutions 3.3.1.Evolution of Local Self- Government and Panchayat Raj in Tamil Nadu Mahatma Gandhi championed village self-governance, an ideal reflected in Article 40 of the Constitution, which directs the State to organise Village Panchayats. Even under British rule, Viceroys Mayo and Ripon promoted local self -government. The 29 29 Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three -tier Panchayat Raj system, implemented from 1960, though PRIs remained weakened by poor representation of SCs, STs and women, and limited powers and finances. Tamil Nadu's tradition of local self - governance dates to inscriptions at the Sri Vaikundavasa Perumal Temple, Uthiramerur (c. 920 A.D., under Parantaka Chola), which record a written constitution for village assemblies with election procedures and eligibility norms. Under the "Kuda Olai Murai," voters wrote candidates' names on palm leaves and dropped them into a mud pot serving as a ballot box —a remarkable democracy within a monarchy and a precursor to modern elections. This system declined under colonial rule. 30 30 Local governance later evolved through the Acts of 1854, 1871 and 1884 (creating District Boards, Taluk Boards and Village Panchayats), the 1920 Acts, and the Madras Village Panchayats Act, 1950. The Madras Panchayats Act, 1958 established a two -tier system of Village Panchayats and Panchayat Unions.

items.text: The Madras Panchayats Act, 1958 established a two -tier system of Village Panchayats and Panchayat Unions. The 73 rd Constitutional Amendment (1993) gave Panchayats constitutional status, and the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Act, 1994 created a th ree-tier system with directly elected members, reservations for SCs/STs and women (50% since 2016), a State Election Commission, State Finance Commissions and District Planning Committees. Functions related to all 29 Eleventh Schedule subjects have been devolved, making Panchayats vital active agents for grassroots development. 31 31 3.3.2.Panchayat Raj System The Panchayat Raj System in Tamil Nadu functions through a constitutionally mandated three -tier structure comprising District Panchayats, Block (Panch ayat Union) Panchayats, and Village Panchayats. Each tier performs distinct yet complementary functions within the framework of rural governance, while the devolution of financial resources follows the principle of subsidiarity, ensuring that the largest share of funds is allocated to Village Panchayats, where essential public services are delivered directly to citizens. items.text: Block Panchayats provide technical coordination, programme implementation support, and inter -village infrastructure, while District Panchayats undertake district- level planning, coordination, monitoring, and policy oversight. 33 33 3.3.3 Rural Local Bodies Reorganisation The administrative structure of Rural Local Bodies in Tamil Nadu has evolved continuously in response to demographic growth, administrative convenience, and the need for improved public service delivery. The Govern ment has undertaken periodic reorganisation through the formation of new District Panchayats, Panchayat Unions, and Village Panchayats, merger of Village Panchayats, and upgradation of eligible Village Panchayats into Town Panchayats to strengthen local governance and enhance administrative accessibility. Recent reorganisation include the formation of the Mayiladuthurai District Panchayat, establishment of nine new Panchayat Unions, constitution of ninety - three new Village Panchayats, merger of 34 34 two Village Panchayats in Kanyakumari District, and upgradation of Gandarvakottai Village Panchayat into a Town Panchayat. Village Panchayats across the State vary considerably in terms of population, geographical characteristics, settlement patterns, and development potential. While most Village Panchayats have a population between 1,000 and 5,000, several have populations exceeding 10,000 and require urban-like civic infrastructure. Further, villages with special characteristics such as coastal, hilly, and tourism areas require differentiated planning, specialised infrastructure, environmental safeguards, and context -specific development interventions. 35 35 3.4.Powers and Functions of the Panchayat Raj Institutions 3.4.1.Village Panchayats Tamil Nadu has 12,571 Village Panchayats comprising 78,997 habitations spread across 37 rural districts.

items.text: 35 35 3.4.Powers and Functions of the Panchayat Raj Institutions 3.4.1.Village Panchayats Tamil Nadu has 12,571 Village Panchayats comprising 78,997 habitations spread across 37 rural districts. The President of the Village Panchayat is its Executive Authority, and unless dissolved in accordance with law, every Village Panchayat continues in office for fiv e years from the date appointed for its first meeting after an ordinary election. Village Panchayat-wise rural population data based on Census 2011—covering total, SC, ST and women population—were published in August 2014 in coordination with the Director of Census Operations and are available on the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department website. 36 36 3.4.2.Mandatory Functions (Section 110) Every Village Panchayat shall, within its jurisdiction, undertake: • Construction, repair and maintenance of village roads (other than Highways and Panchayat Union Roads), with connected bridges, culverts and causeways; • Street lighting in residential areas; construction and maintenance of drainage and arrangements for its disposal; 37 37 • Street cleaning and public sanitation through Solid Waste Management; provision and maintenance of public latrines; • Provision and maintenance of burial and cremation grounds; Supply and distribution of safe drinking water; sinking and maintenance of wells, ponds and other water bodies; • Maintenance and preservation of community assets vested in the Panchayat, and other duties imposed by the Government by notification. 3.4.3.
