The Access to the Sujalam Bharath Mobile Application is provided to the following limited users: • State level: Nodal Officer; Chairman of Executive Committee; Chief Engineer, JJM • District level: District Collectors; ACs/ PDs – DRDA; EEs of TWAD Board Upon successful geo-tagging/ geo- referencing and approval, “Sujal Gaon IDs” are generated. These habitation -level identifiers provide comprehensive information on piped water supply assets from source to habitation. 192 192 7.2.8. User Fee Charges:

User Fee Charges: The Village Panchayat will be responsible for the Operation and Maintenance of the Water Supply. • Minimum User Charge of ₹30/- is being collected. • The Bulk water transfer charges to the TWAD Board has to be paid by the Village Panchayats at the tariff rate fixed by the Government. • Water Supply Works under Jal Jeevan Mission are monitored by Village Water Supply and Sanitatio n Committee – (VWSC) and Village Panchayat. 7.2.9. Internet of Things (IoT): Automatic sensor-based monitoring & control system improves the efficient usage of electricity and public water supply systems. This prevents unwarranted 193 193 wastage of water through controlled usage of the motor. The Automatic sensor-based Monitoring systems were installed in few Panchayats and will be scaled up in a phased manner. 7.3.Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) -SBM(G) The Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) [SBM(G)] was launched to eliminate open defecation through behavioural change and the construction of Individual Household Latrines (IHHLs) and Community Sanitary Complexes (CSCs) . Under SBM(G) Phase I (2014– 2019), Tamil Nadu achieved Open Defecation Free (ODF) status in 2019, with all Village Panchayats declared ODF.

items.text: Under SBM(G) Phase I (2014– 2019), Tamil Nadu achieved Open Defecation Free (ODF) status in 2019, with all Village Panchayats declared ODF. Phase II, launched in 2020– 21, focuses on ODF Plus , emphasizing the sustainability of ODF status, effective Solid 194 194 and Liquid Waste Management (SLWM), and the creation of visually clean villages. Except for IHHLs and Faecal Sludge Management (FSM) , all programme components are implemented in convergence with Finance Commission Grants and other schemes. SBM(G) is a key enabler for achieving the Localized Sustainable Development Goals (LSDGs) by strengthening Rural Local Bodies, improving sanitation services, promoting sustainable waste management, and enhancing environmental sustainability. The Mission primarily contributes to SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation) while also supporting SDGs 3, 11, 12, and 13 through improved public health, resource efficiency, and climate resilience. 195 195 7.3.1. Components of SBM (G) -II Swachh Bharat Mission (Gram in) Phase II have four important components. A. ODF sustainability : 100% access to Safe Sanitation to all through construction of Individual Household Latrines, Community Sanitary Complexes and IEC activities. B. Solid Waste Management: Effective management of solid waste by at least 80% of households and all public places. To ensure the construction and proper functioning of infrastructure related to the management of biodegradable and non- biodegradable waste. Also, construction of plastic waste management units as well as GoBARdhan plants, with a focus on their functionality. 196 196 C. Liquid Waste Management:

Also, construction of plastic waste management units as well as GoBARdhan plants, with a focus on their functionality. 196 196 C. Liquid Waste Management: Coverage of at least 80% of Households and all Public Places with Grey Water Management, Black Water Management (Wastewater containing faecal matter). D. Visual Cleanliness of the villages: Villages are visually clean with minimal litter, minimal Stagnant Water and No Plastic dump. 7.3.2. Categorisation of Village Panchayats The Village Panchayats are given star rating under SBM- G Phase II based on the saturation in above components. This assessment is used to measure the progress achieved by each village panchayat in Open Defecation Free (ODF) sustainability, solid waste management, liquid waste management and visual 197 197 cleanliness and to facilitate continuous improvement. 7.3.3. Individual Household Latrines (IHHL) The scheme aims to ensure that a ll rural families can access safe toilets. A duly completed IHHL shall consist of a sanitary substructure, a superstructure, and a water 198 198 storage facility to ensure proper hygiene. Identified eligible households are given an incentive of ₹ 12,000/- for const ructing IHHLs. So far, in phase II, 6,83,782 IHHLs have been taken up with an outlay of ₹780.30 crore under SBM (G) for those who have not been covered under earlier schemes. 7.3.4.

Community Sanitary Complexes (CSC) An ODF Plus village is expected to have at least one community sanitary complex, which may cater to the sanitation needs of the floating population. The CSCs have separate facilities for men and women and consist of an appropriate number of toilet seats, including one for the physically challenged, bathing cubicles, running water and wash basins. It is built in a place in the village that is acceptable and accessible. 16,317 Community Sanitary Complexes 199 199 were taken up with an outlay of ₹642.08 crore under SBM(G) Phase II in convergence with Finance Commission Grant and other schemes. 7.4.Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) has significantly strengthened rural road connectivity in Tamil Nadu through successive phases. Under PMGSY-I, all-weather road connectivity was provided to 1,986 unconnected habitations by constructing and upgrading 7,678 roads covering 16,296 km and 98 bridges at a cost of ₹ 4,586 crore. Under PMGSY -II, 860 road s covering 2,940 km and 34 bridges were upgraded at a cost of ₹1,434 crore.

items.text: Under PMGSY -II, 860 road s covering 2,940 km and 34 bridges were upgraded at a cost of ₹1,434 crore. Under PMGSY-III (2019–20 to 2024– 25), 1,826 roads covering 7,377 km and 83 bridges 200 200 were sanctioned at a cost of ₹4,875 crore to improve connectivity to Gramin Agricultural Markets, Higher Secondary Schools, and Hospitals. Under PMGSY-IV, the focus is on providing all -weather road connectivity to the remaining eligible unconnected habitations with a population of 500 and above in plain areas and 250 and above in hilly areas , based on the 2011 Census . Tamil Nadu has almost achieved universal rural habitation connectivity, with only 9 eligible habitations in forest areas remaining. Forest clearance has been obtained for 4 habitations , and action is underway to secure statutory clearances for the remaining 5 habitations. 201 201 7.4.1. PM-JANMAN PM-JANMAN aims at providing road connectivity to unconnected Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group (PVTG) habitations having population of more than 100. During 2025-26, sanction has been accorded for the construction of 4 roads covering a length of 10.96 Km at a cost of ₹9.07 crore to provide connectivity to 5 tribal habitations. 7.4.2.Maintenance of PMGSY Roads The maintenance of PMGSY roads is being monitored through the Electronic Maintenance of Rural Roads (e -MARG) portal of the Government of India. As per PMGSY guide lines, maintenance of PMGSY roads is fully funded by State Government.

items.text: As per PMGSY guide lines, maintenance of PMGSY roads is fully funded by State Government. During 2025 -26, an amount of ₹ 45 crore was allocated by the State 202 202 Government towards maintenance of PMGSY roads. During 2026 -27, an amount of ₹50 crore is required for routine maintenance of 7,178 Km length of PMGSY roads. 7.4.3. Performance Incentive Grant Government of India introduced Performance Incentive Grants for States based on their performance under PMGSY. From 2016 -17 to 2024- 25, Tamil Nadu has received Incentive Grants amounting to ₹356 crore. The State Government has provided a matching share of ₹237 crore. The funds are utilised for periodic renewal of PMGSY roads that have completed the prescribed maintenance period. So far, periodic renewal works have been carried out for 4,972 Km length of PMGSY roads under this initiative. 203 203 7.4.4.Technology Initiatives Tamil Nadu has been a pioneer in adopting innovative and environment - friendly technologies in rural road construction. Technologies such as Cement Stabilisation, Soil Stabilisation, Coir Technology, Chemical Stabilisation, Waste Plastic Roads and Cold Mix Technology have been adopted under PMGSY. From 2012 -13 to 2024- 25, roads covering a length of 6,175 Km at a cost of ₹3,666 crore have been taken up using various alternate technologies. Tamil Nadu received recognition from the Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India for outstanding implementation of road construction works using green and innovative technologies during the 25th Anniversary celebrations of PMGSY during 2026.

The scheme provides a unit assistance of ₹ 1.20 lakh per house, shared between the Union and State Governments in the ratio of 60:40, with a minimum plinth area of 269 sq. ft. To ensure the construction of durable houses, the State Government provides an additional ₹1.20 lakh per house towards RCC roofing and related costs. Beneficiaries also receive ₹12,000/- for toilets under SBM-G, 90 person -days of unskilled wages under MGNREGS/VB GRAM , and access to loans of up to ₹70,000/-, if required. 205 205 From 2016–17 to 2024 –25, 7,02,560 houses have been sanct ioned, of which 6,68,709 houses have been completed. The Government of India has released ₹5,058 crore, while the State Government has contributed ₹3,372 crore as its matching share.

items.text: The Government of India has released ₹5,058 crore, while the State Government has contributed ₹3,372 crore as its matching share. In addition, the State has released ₹5,283 crore towards RCC roofing assistance, with an expenditure of ₹5,066 crore, ensuring the timely completion of quality rural housing. 7.6.Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN) During 2023-24 the Ministry of Tribal Welfare, Government of India has launched a scheme PM-JANMAN (Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan) to improve the socio-economic condition of the Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs). Providing pucca houses to the 206 206 PVTG households is one of the interventions by MoRD, GoI under PM-JANMAN. In Tamil Nadu, six tribal communities viz., Irular, Kattunayakkan, Kota, Korumba, Paniyann and Toda residing in 21 Districts are eligible to get houses under this scheme. To provide PVTG households and habitations with basic facilities such as safe housing, clean drinking water and sanitation, improved access to education, health and nutrition, road and telecom connectivity, and sustainable livelihood opportunities on saturation mode. A housing scheme for PVTGs, similar to PMAY-G with slight modifications, has been approved by the Ministry of Rural Development, Government of India. 207 207 7.6.1.

Mode of Selection of beneficiaries Based on the list of PVTG villages provided by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, the Ministry of Rural Development has mapped these villages on the Awaas portal, and eligible households are identified through village-level surveys conducted via the AwaasApp. After completing the surveys, houses have been sanctioned to eligible PVTG households following due procedures. Owning a p ucca house and having a Government Employee as a member in the family are the two exclusion criteria under this scheme. 7.6.2.Plinth Area and Unit Cost (State Support to PM-JANMAN) The State Government has increased the plinth area of 269 sq.ft to 300 sq.ft in Tamil Nadu.

The unit cost of a house under PM-JANMAN in Tamil Nadu is ₹5.07 lakh per 208 208 house for Plains and ₹5.73 lakh for hilly area which is inclusive of State support cost, convergence with MGNREGS/VB-GRAM wages for 90 person -days of un -skilled labour over and above the unit cost, and assistance of ₹12,000/- for toilets through convergence with the Swachh Bharat Mission – Gramin (SBM-G) 7.6.3.Sanction and Fund Allocation Houses are sanctioned under the Pradhan Mantri Janjati Adivasi Nyaya M aha Abhiyan, with an enhanced plinth area of 300 sq.ft and substantial additional assistance from the State, under which 13,065 houses have been sanctioned at an estimated cost of ₹261 crore. Apart from this, State Support cost provided by Government of Tamil Nadu is ₹367 crore. 209 8. Revised Budget Estimates for 2026-27 211 211 8. Revised Budget Estimates for 2026-27 A sum of ₹39,609 crore is provided in the Revised Budget Estimate for the year 2026-27 out of which, the revenue Expenditure is ₹ 33,971 crore and Ca pital Expenditure is ₹5,638 crore. 213 9.Conclusion 215 215 9.Conclusion Tamil Nadu has established one of the most robust and progressive systems of rural local governance in the country.

items.text: 213 9.Conclusion 215 215 9.Conclusion Tamil Nadu has established one of the most robust and progressive systems of rural local governance in the country. With a network comprisi ng 37 rural districts, 37 District Panchayats, 397 Block Panchayats, 12,571 Village Panchayats, and 78,997 habitations, serving a rural population of more than four crore citizens , the State possesses a strong institutional platform for advancing inclusive and sustainable rural development. Over the past three decades, the evolving developmental landscape has brought forth new challenges, including fragmented scheme -based planning, increasing maintenance liabilities, misalignment of administrative boundaries, rapid peri-urbanisation, limited institutional convergence, and the growing need for 216 216 digital governance and climate -resilient infrastructure. The policy proposals presented in this Concept Note collectively address these emerging challenges through a comprehensive and integrated reform agenda under the vision of "Vetri Tamizhagam." The proposed interventions seek to strengthen Village Panchayats as vibrant institutions of local self -government capable of delivering efficient public services, promoting in clusive economic growth, fostering participatory democracy, and ensuring sustainable management of public assets. The introduction of transformative initiatives such as New Housing scheme, the Tamil Nadu Village Empowerment, Transformation and Rejuvenation Initiative (TN -VETRI), the Panchayat 217 217 Development Index , category -specific development missions, digital Gram Sabha platforms, enhanced fiscal devolution, strengthened infrastructure maintenance, and institutional capacity building together provide a compr ehensive roadmap for the future of rural governance in Tamil Nadu.
items.source: Tamil Nadu Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department: Policy Note 2026-27 [Rural Development and Panchayat Raj department]
items.title: Tamil Nadu Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department: Policy Note 2026-27

items.text: Implementation of these recommendations, supported by the proposed financial framework and phased resource mobilisation strategy, would enable the State to transition from fragmented programme implementation towards a unified, outcome -oriented, and citizen-centric model of rural development. Such an integrated approach would not only improve governance and public service delivery but also accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Developme nt Goals, strengthen local democracy, promote 218 218 resilient rural economies, and realise the vision of "Vetri Tamizhagam" —creating digitally empowered, self -reliant, prosperous, and sustainable rural communities across Tamil Nadu. Introduction With more than 43 lakh registered Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), Tamil Nadu's MSME sector contributes approximately 30% to the State's industrial output and accounts for about 46% of its total exports. Tamil Nadu is the third -largest MSME ecosystem in India, that accounts for roughly 15% of the nation's total MSMEs. These enterprises generate around 3.20 crore jobs and are a m ajor driver of the State's manufacturing GDP and exports. The Economic Survey 2025 -26 points out that , Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) sector has positioned itself as the backbone of the India’s 2 2 industrial economy, driving over 31.1% of Gross Do mestic Product (GDP) in the country, 35.4% of manufacturing output, and over 48.58% of exports in India. With over 7.47 crore enterprises employing over 32.82 crore persons, the sector holds its position as the second-largest employer next to agriculture. Globally, MSMEs make up about 90 percent of businesses and are responsible for over 50 percent of the total global employment. With India’s manufacturing sector positioned for greater global integration, MSME sector’s role is critical in enabling effectiv e supply -chain participation, fostering local value addition, and supporting inclusive regional growth, the survey has stated.

items.text: Udyam Registration The registration on ‘Udyam’ portal gives recognition to MSMEs and make them eligible to avail benefits under various incentives including capital subsidy and interest subventions on loans as per MSME policy 2021. 5 As of 30 th June 2026, the category wise distribution of MSMEs under Udyam registration is given below:- Category No. of MSMEs Percentage Micro 42,97,232 98.83% Small 46,814 1.08% Medium 3,936 0.09% Total 43,47,982 100% 1.2. Core Industrial Clusters The Stat e's MSME sector is highly diversified, producing over 6,000 varieties of products. Major manufacturing clusters are concentrated heavily in Chennai, Coimbatore, Tiruppur, and Kancheepuram. With 32% entrepreneurs being women, the sector is an authenticatio n to the State’s inclusive growth and encouraging business environment. 6 6 The state’s aspiring entrepreneurs, its skilled workforce and the progressive policies implemented by the Government of Tamil Nadu attribute to the growth of MSMEs in the State. The policies/ schemes, implemented by the Government of Tamil Nadu have also helped to sustain the targets under the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially to; SDG 5: Achieve gender equality and empower all women 7 SDG 8: Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all. SDG 9: Build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization and foster innovation. 1.3.

It is being executed through the Commissionerate of Industries and Commerce and the Tamil Nadu Small 51 Industries Development Corporation (TANSIDCO). Tamil Nadu Trade Receivables Discounting System (TN-TReDS): Delay in payments is one of the biggest issues currently being faced by MSME vendors. Such delay locks up or blocks the working capita l of MSMEs. To address this issue and expedite the process of receiving payment for their goods and services supplied to Tamil Nadu Government controlled entities, TN -TReDS, an ERP for discounting trade receivables integrated with TReDS was developed and launched. As on 31.05.2026, 99 Public Sector Enterprises have been onboarded on the platform along with their 2220 MSME vendors and invoices of 1581 MSMEs, to the tune of Rs.6265.59 crore have been discounted. 63 2.5.6. Tamil Nadu Credit Guarantee Scheme (TNCGS) To improve access to formalised credit for Micro and Small Enterprises, the Tamil Nadu Credit Guarantee Scheme (TNCGS) was launched. The scheme, while operating with the ext ent Credit Guarantee Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) of the Government of India, provides 90% guarantee coverage for collateral free loans up to Rs.40 lakh and up to 80% for loans above Rs.40 lakh and upto Rs.2 crore. TNCGS also provides Standalone guarantee coverage of 90% for loans upto Rs.40 lakh to manufacturing enterprises.

Tamil Nadu Industry Database In order to create a comprehensive and reliable Industrial Information Database for the State, the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Department has developed the Tamil Nadu Industrial Database Mobil e Application (TN Thozhil Tharavu Thalam) in coordination with NIC. The application facilitates collection, updation and validation of industrial unit information through mobile-based OTP authentication and geo-location capture. The database will serve as a vital repository of industrial information and assist the Government in formulating focused policies, strengthening industrial outreach and delivering need -based support services to MSMEs. 65 As part of the development of the Tamil Nadu Industrial Databa se, a total of 46,01,603 mapped and unmapped industrial unit records have been consolidated and integrated into the platform from various data sources. The database is being continuously enriched through field-level updation and verification by the District Industries Centres and Entrepreneurs. The platform facilitates identification and validation of industrial units and supports the creation of a robust Industrial Information Ecosystem, thereby enabling evidence -based policy formulation, targeted interventions and improved service delivery for the growth of the MSME sector in Tamil Nadu. 65 64 13,000 women, 2 ,000 SC/ STs and 61 differently abled entrepreneurs.

Functioning with the primary objective of creating sustainable livelihood opportunities for members of the Irula community engaged in snake -catching activities, the Society currently comprises 329 members. The Society undertakes the collection of snake venom through scientific extraction methods and supplies the same to 79 research institutions and pharmaceutical laboratories to produce anti -venom and related research purposes. Through its activities, the Society plays a significant role in generating continuous employment and enhancing the socio -economic well -being of its members. Considering the hardships faced by the members in trapping snakes, the snake-trapping charges have been increased considerably with effect from 2024. Consequent to this and considering the rise in operational costs, the selling pric e of snake venom has also been increased from February 2025. As a result, during the financial year 2025 –26, the Society sold 338.950 grams of snake venom and realized a revenue of Rs.2.42 crore. Plots/ Sheds/ Modules Allotment Policy Developed plots/ sheds/ modules in TANSIDCO Industrial Est ates are being allotted on outright sale/ lease/ rental basis 114 114 to MSMEs by advertising the details of vacant plots/ sheds/ modules in the official website of TANSIDCO. On receipt of application requesting allotment of plots/ sheds/ modules, a Screening Com mittee meeting is convened to select eligible applicants. In case of high number of eligible applicants, allotment is made through draw of lots in the presence of the applicants. Timeline for execution of Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and handing over of plot have been reduced from 2 months to 15 days. To facilitate the MSMEs in commencing production early, interim loans are arranged for purchase of TANSIDCO plots/ sheds under the Industrial Infrastructure Initiative Scheme (IIIS) of Tamil Nadu Industr ial Investment Corporation (TIIC); and the Flexi Loan for Your MSME (FLY -MSME) of the Tamil Nadu Industrial Co -operative Bank (TAICO Bank). 115 3.8.2. e-Governance initiatives TANSIDCO has computerised its operations to provide faster and efficient services to MSMEs. Patta for Industrial plots 41 Government Industrial Estates and 100 TANSIDCO owned Industrial Estates were formed through transfer of land / alienation from Government and other ways. The classi fications of these lands are recorded in the revenue records as Sarkar Poromboke in most Industrial Estates and as Ryotwari in a few Industrial Estates. Hence, MSMEs could not get the patta for these lands. To address this issue, the Government formed an empowered committee headed by the Chief Secretary to change the classification of the land from Sarkar Poramboke to Ryotwari lands. As a result, the Government issued order for change the classification of 2053 acres of Government 119 Poromboke land as Ryotwari in 23 Government Industrial Estates and 26 SIDCO Industrial Estates. As on date, 9,970 unit holders have been issued with NOC for getting patta easily and 3,825 allottees benefited by obtaining the patta for their Industrial Plots. 3.8.4.

items.text: It was established in the year 2001 under the Societies Registration Act as a non -profit organization. The primary objective of the Institute is to create a robust ecosystem for entrepreneurship and innovation across Tamil Nadu. The core activities of the Entrepreneurship D evelopment and Innovation Institute include providing training in collaboration with Government Departments, conducting various skill -based entrepreneurship development programs, 128 128 promoting innovation, and offering business and commercial consultancies. Th ese activities create an enabling environment to transform entrepreneurs and aspiring entrepreneurs into successful business leaders. Additionally, this institute supports the establishment of Incubation Centres and conducts hackathons to foster entrepreneurial and innovative thinking among school and higher education students. Since its inception, the institute has provided training, guidance, and seed funding to over five lakh diverse beneficiaries, including aspiring micro, small, and medium entrepreneu rs and startups through various schemes. Over the past four years, awareness and training on entrepreneurship and innovation have been provided to 42 lakh school students through the School Innovation Development Project 129 (SIDP) and to 11 lakh higher educ ation students through the Tamil Nadu Youth Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Programme (TNYIEDP). Strategies The institute promotes entrepreneurship and innovation in Tamil Nadu through the following activities: ● Enhancing the entrepreneurial skills of aspiring youth and entrepreneurs ● Creating infrastructure and providing seed funding support for technology and startups ● Integrating formal entrepreneurship education into schools and higher education institutions, and organizing Hackathons 129 128 promoting innovation, and offering business and commercial consultancies. Th ese activities create an enabling environment to transform entrepreneurs and aspiring entrepreneurs into successful business leaders.

Entrepreneurship Development Training Programmes Entrepreneurship development training and various skill -based business development programs are conducted in collaboration with variou s Government Departments. These training sessions are organized across diverse topics, such as identifying business opportunities, market analysis, business plan preparation, business model generation, Strength, Weakness, Opportunities, and Challenges (SWO C) analysis, risk management, and legal procedures for setting up a business enterprise. 133 5.1.1. Entrepreneurship Development Programme (Coordination) This institute provides entrepreneurship development training to selected beneficiaries in coordinati on with various Government Departments and organizations, such as the Commissionerate of Industries and Commerce (IC&DIC), Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (TNCDW), Tamil Nadu Skill Development Corporation (TNSDC), Tamil Nadu State Rural Liv elihoods Mission (TNSRLM), Tamil Nadu Urban Livelihoods Mission (TNULM), Tamil Nadu Food Processing and Agri Export Promotion Corporation (TNAPEx), Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board (TNUHDB), Tamil Nadu Adi Dravidar Housing and Development Corpor ation (TAHDCO) and The National Institute for Entrepreneurship & Small Business Development (NIESBUD). 134 134 In the financial year 2025 -26, in-person training was provided to 19,925 beneficiaries under the above schemes at an estimated cost of Rs.3.39 crore.

Furthermore, online training was provided to 2,440 beneficiaries under the New Entrepreneur cum Enterprise Development Scheme (NEEDS), and to 1,581 beneficiaries under the Annal Ambedkar Business Champions Scheme (AABCS). In the financial year 2025 -26, a total of 6,601 beneficiaries were provided with online entrepreneurship development training. 135 5.1.2. Skill-Based Entrepreneurship Development Programme (SBEDP) The Entrepreneurship Development and Innovation Institute (EDII) is implementing the Skill-Based Entrepreneurship Development Programme (SBEDP) in second- and third -tier cities across Tamil Nadu. Under this programme, beneficiaries who are interested in starting enterprises are identified and selected. Based on their needs, skill trainin g is provided, along with support for Udyam registration, business facilitation services, and continuous mentoring to help them establish and sustain their enterprises. During the financial year 2025 –26, a total of 231 training programmes were conducted, b enefiting 9,000 participants. Among them, 1,460 beneficiaries have successfully started their own enterprises.

items.text: The 'Nimir ndhu Nil' Tamil Nadu Youth Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Programme (TNYIEDP) is a 138 138 flagship initiative of the Government of Tamil Nadu. This scheme is implemented using a Hub and Spoke model with the objective of creating an entrepreneurial mindset and startup culture among higher education students and youth in Tamil Nadu. Moreover, to encourage students' innovative ideas, the 'Nimir ndhu Nil' Hackathon is conducted, through which selected innovative concepts are awarded cash prizes and seed funding. Under this scheme, 2,000 higher education institutions across Tamil Nadu have been connected, including universities, engineering, arts and science colleges, polytechnics, industrial training institutes (ITIs), as well as agriculture, veterinary, fisheries, and medical colleges. The schem e is being implemented at an estimated cost of Rs.19.57 crore, with the objective of creating 139 around 10,000 student entrepreneurs over a 5-year period from 2025 to 2030. In the financial year 2025 -26, awareness and training were provided to 3,04,300 studen ts at an estimated cost of Rs.3.55 crore. 5.2.2. The major activities and initiatives undertaken by FaMeTN are as follows. 6.1. Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance (RAMP) FaMeTN is the State Nodal Agency for the RAMP Scheme, a Central Sector S cheme 152 152 of the Ministry of MSME, Government of India. Rs.165 crore has been earmarked for Tamil Nadu over four years for initiatives including Digital MSME Facilitation Services, Industry Transformation Maps, Vendor Development Programmes, International Reverse Buyer -Seller Meets, Quality Certifications and Intellectual Property Rights. So far, Rs.43.57 crore has been utilised for these projects, which are at various stages of implementation. 6.2. Access to Markets Limited market access and business visibility remain key challenges for MSMEs. To overcome these barriers, FaMeTN implements focused initiatives that facilitates participation in trade fairs and exhibitions, promotes digital commerce, strengthens buyer-seller linkages and enhances access to Government procurement opportunities, 153 thereby improving the competitiveness and growth prospects of MSMEs.

The State’s sustained investments in health, nutrition, education, social protection and gender equality have contributed to improved human development outcomes and strengthened the overall social well -being of its people. The State has been a consistent top performer with 'Front Runner' status in the majority of the Sustainable Development Goals and continues to perform exceptionally well in areas such as decent work, reduced inequalities and inclusive communities. Tamil Nadu is witnessing significant demographic and socio -economic transformation, with evolving family structures, rising participation of women in the workforce, growing demand for child care, increasing elderly population and inclusive communities. In this 3 context, the Social Welfare and Women Empowerment Department through its interventions, assists the vulnerable segments to address the evolving challenges on account of these changes .

These schemes create an enabling ecosystem that empowers women to realise their full potential and contribute meaningfully to the State's economic and social progress. 15 1.1.1 Tamil Nadu State Policy for Women Tamil Nadu State Policy for Women focuses on boosting female workforce participation, digital literacy, ensuring equal rights to education, healthcare, employment and political participation. 1.1.2 Women Helpline The women helpline provides 24*7 telecom support services to women through the toll -free number 181. In Tamil Nadu, 59 OSCs are functioning, across all the 38 districts. These centres provide comprehensive support services including temporary shelter, medical assistance, psychological counselling, free legal aid, police assistance and referral services to the affected women and their children (girls of all ages and boys up to 12 years ). The OSCs are integrated with the Women Helpline (181). The OSCs are provided with dedicated vehicles for emergency outreach and rescue operations. 17 A sum of Rs.18.62 crore has been allocated in the Revised Budget Estimate for the year 2026–27. 1.1.4 Shelter and accommodation facilities for women i. Short Stay Homes To restore dignity, instil confidence and improve social security for women affected by abandonment, exploitation and social distress, short stay homes (sakthi sadan) are run through voluntary organizations. The women in these homes are provided food, clothing, counselling, medical care, legal assistance, vocational training and rehabilitation services. In Tamil Nadu, 46 such homes are functioning, which are funded under the Mission Shakthi’s Samarthya Scheme with a funding pattern of 60:40 between the Central and State Government. 17 16 A sum of Rs.69 lakh has been allocated in the Revised Budget Estimate for the year 2026-27.

The Commission is headed by a chairperson and supported by nine members. It examines matters relating to the constitutional and legal safeguards available to women and monitors their effective implementation. The Commission also reviews existing laws and policy provisions affecting women and recommends suitable amendments and remedial measures to strengthen the protection of women's rights. As part of its mandate, the Commission takes up cases involving violations of constitutional and legal provisions relating to women with the appropriate authorities. It also takes suo motu cognizance of issues concerning the non -implementation of law provisions intended to protect women. items.text: To honour Perunthalaivar Kamarajar for his pioneering initiative of providing meals to children in school with a view of promoting education, the C hief Minister’s Breakfast S cheme has been named as Perunthalaivar Kamarajar Breakfast Scheme. 35 The scheme cover s 19.34 lakh students in classes I to V, across 37,447 schools. In the current year 2026 -27, the scheme is being expanded to cover 15,14,274 students studying in classes VI to VIII in 15,454 Government and Government-aided schools. The eligibility criteria for the schemes are relaxed to include transgender who have completed schooling from private schools and non-Tamil medium. At present 35 transgender persons are receiving monthly incentive under this scheme. 53 52 1.4.6 Short Stay Homes Transgender persons commute from one place to another for various purposes, including education, skill training, employment, medical treatment, meetings and workshops. During such journeys, they face considerable difficulties in securing safe, dignified and affordable accommodation, particularly when an overnight stay is required. To address this need and ensure their safety, dignity and well -being, Short Stay Homes for Transgender Persons will be established in 15 districts, providing safe, accessible and supportive accommodation for short-term stay. 1.4.7 Free Bus Travel The free bus travel scheme is being implemented to enable transgender persons to have easy access to education, health care and other social opportunities. 53 1.4.8 Higher Education Assistance Financial assistance is extended to transgender persons to ensure that they pursue higher education without interruption. College expenses such as tuition fees, hostel fees and related educational expenses are covered. So far, a sum of Rs. 21.80 lakh have been spent for 24 transgender students. Launched in 1975, ICDS has emerged as one of the world’s largest and most comprehensive early childhood care and development programmes. It addresses the multifaceted challenges faced by vulnerable and marginalized communities. The scheme is implemented through a vast network of anganwadi centres, where anganwadi workers and anganwadi helpers serve as the frontline functionaries, acting as the primary interface 59 between the community and the service delivery system.

Jan Andolan, implemented under the National Nutrition Mission, is a comprehensive awareness and community -based initiative approach aimed at taking nutrition -related information to every household. The movement is taken forward with the participation of local body representatives, State Government Departments, community based organisations and stakeholders from both public and private sectors. Necessary funds have been provided to districts to conduct samudaya valaikappu programmes, World Breastfeeding Week celebration, traditional food festivals, nutrition month and nutrition fortnight , awareness exhibitions at the State, District and Block levels, health and nutrition education to adolescent girls workshops and training programmes for anganwadi workers. 71 3.1.3 Non-Formal Pre School Education Early childhood (0 -6 years) is a critical and formative phase in a child’s life laying the foundation of holistic development. Learning begins at birth, and experiences during these early years provide the base for all subsequent learning and Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) plays a significant role in the learning process of the child in this stage. Aadi Paadi Vilaiyadu Pa apa (APVP) programme is a specialized curriculum implemented in the State in alignment with the National Early Childhood Care and Education Policy, 2013. This developmental age-appropriate and contextualized annual curriculum has been designed for the holistic development of the children. The curriculum comprises preschool activities with 11 child -friendly theme -based modules for 11 months.

The Directorate implements and coordinates the enforcement of the following major legislations relating to the care, protection, welfare and rehabilitation of children: • The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 • The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 • The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005 • The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 • The Tamil Nadu Prevention of Begging Act, 1945 The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015, is an umbrella act which aims to protect and support children towards meeting 85 their basic needs and providing for their education, development, rehabilitation and various other interventions. It prescribes mechanisms for the overall well -being of children through appropriate institutions, services and support systems. It establishes statutory and institutional mechanisms such as Child Welfare Committees (CWCs), Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs), District Child Protection Units (DCPUs) and Special Juvenile Police Units (SJPUs). The Act provides for specific interventions towards two categories of children viz Children in need of Care and Protection (CNCP) and Children in Conflict with Law (CCL). Children who are orphaned, abandoned, abused, neglected, living on the streets or otherwise without adequate parental care are considered as Children in Need of Care and Protection.

The juvenile justice system adopts a reformative and rehabilitative approach, focusing on education, counselling, skill development and social reintegration. To support implementation of the Juvenile Justice Act, various measures are taken up by both Central and State Governments through various schemes and programmes such as Mission Vatsalya, Child Helpline (1098), Anbu Karangal scheme etc. The Tamil Nadu Juvenile Justice Fund was established under Section 105 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, with an initial corpus of Rs. 25 lakh to support the care, rehabilitation and welfare of Children in Need of Care and Protection (CNCP) and Children in Conflict with Law (CCL). The corpus presently has Rs.77.28 lakh. For the effective administration of the Fund, the Government of Tamil Nadu has framed the Tamil Nadu Juvenile Justice Fund Rules, 2017. 87 To ensure the collection and maintenance of comprehensive and reliable data on the protection and development of children under the Juvenile Justice System, a web -based Child Protection Information Management and Monitoring System (CPIMMS) has been developed. The system facilitates data sharing among stakeholders and supports the effective monitoring and strengthening of various services and schemes for children.

Child Welfare Committees (CWCs) Child Welfare Committees are statutory bodies constituted under the Juvenile Justice Act to deal with matters relating to Children in Need of Care and Protection. The Committees inquiries and ensures that children receive appropriate care, protection, rehabilitation and support through institutional and non -institutional services. 89 The Committees conduct inquiries, arranges suitable care i.e. foster care or institutional placement, and make efforts to restore children to their families. They also deal with orphaned, abandoned and surrendered children and take steps for their adoption. The Committees regularly inspect child care institutions and ensures the safety and well -being of the children, and take suitable action in case they find anything adverse.

Sponsorship Scheme under Mission Vatsalya provides financial support to vulnerable children to prevent family separation and promote family-based care. It covers children of widowed, 104 104 divorced or abandoned mothers, orphaned children living with extended families, children whose parents are affected by serious illness or are unable to provide care. Under preventive sponsorship, children from vulnerable families with an annual family income not exceeding Rs.72,000 in rural areas and Rs.96,000 in urban areas are eligible. They are provided with Rs.4,000 per month until they attain the age of 18 years. With a view to ensure that no deserving vulnerable child is deprived of family -based care and financial support, the Government of Tamil Nadu has introduced the Anbu Karangal Scheme. The scheme provides financial assistance to children who are totally orphaned, have lost one parent and the surviving parent is deserted, or are physically challenged or terminally ill or incarcerated and are being cared for by relatives or other caregivers. Eligible 105 children are provided with Rs. 2,000 per month until they attain the age of 18 years , thereby supporting their continued care within a family environment and preventing institutionalization.

items.text: 4.1.3.2 Adoption Adoption means the process through which the adopted child is permanently separated from his biological parents and becomes the lawful child of his adoptive parents with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities that are attached to a biological child. Orphan, abandoned and surrendered children upon being declared Legally 108 108 Free for Adoption (LFA) by the Child Welfare Committee after due inquiry, are placed for adoption. Prospective adoptive parents register through the Mission Vatsalya portal and undergo a home study by specialised adoption agencies. Eligible children are then referred and matched with suitable prospective adoptive parents, followed by acceptance, pre -adoption foster care and issuance of the adoption order by the District Magistrate. The process is completed with the required documentation and post-adoption follow- up to ensure the child’s safety, well -being and smooth adjustment in the adoptive family. Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) functions under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, the Juvenile Justice Model Rules, 2016, and the Adoption Regulations, 2022 and serves as the national nodal authority for regulating, monitoring and promoting adoption in India. CARA provides 109 the rules, standards and guidelines for in -country and inter -country adoption, maintains the centralised adoption database, regulates online adoption procedures, issues certificates for inter - country adoptions, and supports counselling, training, research and awareness activities. CARA works with SARA, DCPUs, SAAs and other stakeholders to ensure that adoption is carried out in a transparent, child -friendly and legally compliant manner, with proper safeguards and post-adoption support.

items.text: The Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs) conduct inquiries into cases involving children in conflict with law and ensure a child -friendly approach throughout the process. They assess the child’s needs, circumstances and family 112 112 background and provide appropriate care, counselling, education, rehabilitation, and support. The JJBs also pass suitable orders focusing on the child’s reformation, rehabilitation, and social reintegration while protecting their rights, dignity, and best interests. JJBs are established in all the 38 districts. Each Board comprises a Metropolitan Magistrate or First Class Judicial Magistrate and two social worker members of whom at least one is a woman. Further, to provide short and long -term institutional care, protection and rehabilitation services to children in conflict with law, the following homes are established by the Government. Observation Homes are temporary care homes established to provide care and protection to Children in Conflict with Law, whose inquiry is pending before the Juvenile Justice Board. Eight Observation Homes managed by the Government 113 are established in Chennai, Cuddalore, Thanjavur, Trichy, Salem, Coimbatore, Madurai and Tirunelveli. Special Homes are established for the rehabilitation of children found to be in Conflict with Law. Children are placed in such Homes for specific length of time by the order of the Juvenile Justice Board. The children are segregated based on age, gender, nature of offence and their mental and physical status. In Tamil Nadu, two Government Special Homes are functioning, one for boys at Chengalpattu and one for girls at Chennai. Places of Safety are established for Children in Conflict with Law between the age of 16-18 years, accused of or convicted for committing a heinous offence.

items.text: 123 4.3.4 Child Marriage Prevention Child marriage is a serious social concern that affects the education, health, dignity and future opportunities of children. Its prevalence is closely linked with factors such as poverty, social and cultural practices, lack of awareness, school drop-out and vulnerability among children and families. items.text: 135 Chapter 6 Conclusion The Social Welfare and Women Empowerment Department play s a crucial role in advancing the Government of Tamil Nadu’s ambition of furthering a just, inclusive and equitable society. Through a comprehensive range of care, protection, welfare, empowerment and social security interventions, the Department constantly endeavours to address the diverse needs of children, women, senior citizens and transgender persons across different stages of their life. These programmes seek not only to provide support to vulnerable sections but also to strengthen their access to nutrition, education, healthcare, protection, livelihood opportunities and social security thereby enabling them to overcome vulnerabilities and lead lives of dignity and independence. 136 136 These interventions have also contributed significantly to Tamil Nadu’s progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The Department plays a vital role in contributing towards the SDGs by implementing various policies that promote social protection, nutrition, education, equality and the empowerment of vulnerable sections of society. The Department contributes to SDG 1 – No Poverty, through comprehensive social security and livelihood support programmes. Social security pensions benefit more than 3 5 lakh beneficiaries, including destitute and deserted women, senior citizens and transgender persons alleviating poverty and reducing economic vulnerability. Marriage assistance, self - employment and livelihood initiatives further strengthen economic security, while children homes, protection homes for women, senior citizen homes, integrated care complexes and 137 shelter for transgender persons provides care, protection and rehabilitation. These interventions strengthen resilience, promote economic participation and reduce poverty and social exclusion of vulnerable sections. SDG 2 - Zero Hunger, which aims to end hunger, improve nutrition, and ensure food security, is at the core of the Department’s mandate.

PT C.No/3555/2026 Greater Chennai Corporation Revenue Department Dated:04.08.2026 PRESS RELEASE Deduction and Remittance of Profession Tax by Employers The Greater Chennai Corporation informs all Government Departments, Public Sector Undertakings, Local Bodies, Companies, Establishments and other employers functioning within the Chennai Corporation limits that, under Section 117-C of the Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Act, 1998, every employer is legally responsible for deducting Profession Tax from the salary or wages of employees and remitting the same to the Greater Chennai Corporation. As per Rule 277(2) of the Tamil Nadu Urban Local Bodies Rules, 2023, Profession Tax shall be deducted by the employer (Drawing and Disbursing Officer/Employer concerned) from the salary payable through the respective pay bills for the months of August and January every year. CHENNAI METROPOLITAN DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY The Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority (CMDA) is the statutory authority responsible for planning, coordinating and regulating the orderly development of the Chennai Metropolitan Area (CMA). As the State's premier metropolitan planning organisation, CMDA plays a pivotal role in guiding sustainable urban growth through integrated spatial planning, development regulation and strategic infrastructure planning. Initially constituted as an adhoc body in 1972 and accorded statutory status in 1975, CMDA is entrusted with the preparation and implementation of Master Plans, formulation of Development Regulations and execution of key urban development initiatives. The Authority also promotes balanced land use, facilitates infrastructure development, conserves 65 environmentally sensitive areas and supports sustainable economic growth in accordance with contemporary urban planning principles. Through evidence-based planning and coordinated urban governance, CMDA seeks to create a resilient, inclusive and well-connected metropolitan Area, enhancing the quality of life of its residents while supporting the long-term economic development of Tamil Nadu.

Such tenements are being reconstructed with enhanced plinth area in improved and convenient designs by TNUHDB in a phased manner. • The new tenements are allotted to the earlier occupants of the dilapidated tenements. In many of the areas additional tenements are constructed using higher Floor Space Index and are allotted to the extended families of occupants, encroachers and Economically Weaker Section (EWS) families living nearby. 101 Disbursement of grants to facilitate the construction of individual houses on Beneficiary Led Construction mode • The urban poor families having land ownership and living in kutcha houses are given financial grants to construct permanent houses with c oncrete roof on Beneficiary Led Construction mode. Other programmes • All the mud -walled and thatched -roof hutments were upgraded with AC sheet roofs and brick walls on an “as is where is” basis, funded by the State. This large - scale initiative, implemente d in the earlier decades across urban areas of Tamil Nadu, provided slum -dwelling families with protection against the hazards of fire accidents and natural calamities. • Besides, pavement dwellers residing on the arterial roads in Chennai were resettled in developed plots.

items.text: Adoption of Alternate Technology TNUHDB adopts modern construction technology to build tenement s. Techniques such as prefabricated concrete and monolithic concrete construction technologies using aluminium f ormwork, use of light gauge steel frame for doors, windows, UPVC windows and door frames are being adopted for faster construction of safe, sustainable and eco-friendly buildings. 104104 4.3 Programmes implemented during 1970 to 2026 During the years 1970 to 2026 , Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board has constructed 2.83 lakh tenements and 3.59 lakh individual houses have been completed on BLC mode. As part of insitu plotted development programme, TNUHDB has developed and provided 1,37,386 developed plots with land tenure. Besides, developed plots provided to pavements dwellers of Chennai city majority informal houses in urban slum areas have been converted to tiled roof houses. Home improvement loans, slum improvement works, repairs & renewal and refurbishment works and habitation development programmes have been implemented to enhance the living standards of the urban slum families. 105 4.4 Projects Under Implementation The following housing and habitation development programmes are under implementation to achieve the vision of providing affordable housing and enhancing the living standards of the urban poor in Tamil Nadu within a timeframe. 4.4.1 Housing For All (HFA) The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana PMAY (Urban) was formulated to address the housing requirements of urban poor including slum families. As part of this programme , storeyed tenements with basic infrastructure and individual houses on BLC mode are constructed utilizing Government of India, State Government grants and beneficiary contribution.

In cases where societies cannot repay deposits, interest -free loans are provided under this scheme to ensure timely repayment to members. As on 31.03.2026, an amount of Rs.452.78 Lakhs has been accrued in the Fund. • Medium-Term Loan Conversion Over the past 25 years, the societies have experienced a low level of loan disbursement, poor loan recovery and consequently reduced interest income. This has adversely affected their financial stability, resulting in the non-repayment of deposits made by society members, non - payment of salaries to employees, and failure to provide retirement benefits. In these circumstances, societies diverted the 145 income received for its businesses instead of paying back th e loans to the federation causing financial imbalances. To address this, loan accounts are being reconciled, and outstanding amounts are being converted into new medium - term loans to restore financial stability for both the societies and the Federation. Under this scheme, waiver of Penal Interest and EMI interest and 3% interest reduction are provided to the Societies. Only Principal and Interest amount have to be paid by the Societies. The po licy has been approved by the Government in January 2025. CUMTA is further developing a Centralised Parking Information System an intelligent parking management application. CUMTA is hand holding Greater Chennai Corporation in effective Parking planning a nd monitoring the implementation of the Parking Plan for 20 clusters in the first Phase. 7.4.3 Chennai One App: Integrated QR Code Based Ticketing System The project is the first of its kind in India wherein tickets for Suburban Rail System of Southern Ra ilways, Chennai Metro Rail and Metropolitan Transport Corporation Buses are integrated under a single platform ‘Chennai One’ Mobile App . In Chennai a passenger can purchase tickets across multiple modes and make multimodal journey through single payment an d single QR Ticket. The application 165 will provide real -time information to commuters and help them to use multiple public transport services using a single ticket and interchange from one transport service to another. The initiative aims to encourage people to use public transportation and increase its overall share in the transportation system. In the 11 months since its launch (September 2025), more than 20 lakh users have downloaded the app and more than 1 lakh tickets are being booked through the app every day.

TAMIL NADU REAL ESTATE REGULATORY AUTHORITY To promote and regulate the real estate sector efficiently an d transparently , the Real Estate (Regulation & Development) Act of 2016 was enacted , wh ich safeguards the interests of buyers of plots, residential flats and commercial buildings. To enforce this Act in Tamil Nadu, the State Government introduced the Tamil Nadu Real Estate (Regulation & Development) Rules in 2017 and established the Tamil Nadu Real Estate Regulatory Authority (TNRERA), which functions with a Chairperson and two Members. • The key responsibilities of TNRERA include registering real estate proj ects and agents, as well as addressing complaints. Projects involving sales (whether freehold or leasehold), where the land exceeds 500 square meters and includes more than eight apartments (across all phases), must be registered with TNRERA. 174174 • As of June 30 , 2026, TNRERA has registered 35,673 real estate projects and issued registrations to 3,784 real estate agents. It has also admitted 4,851 complaints regarding issues such as delay in handing over possession of houses, structural defects, refunds, and compensation. Of these complaints, final orders have been issued for 3,978 complaints, while 873 are still under review. Conclusion Guided by the vision and policy of the Hon’ble Chief Minister and firmly rooted in the principle that “the welfare of the people is the foremost priority of the Government,” this Government remains committed to ensuring simplicity, efficiency, transparency, accountability and corruption-free governance at every level. Through planned urban growth and people-centred development, the Government is 175 committed to improving the quality of life, ensuring equitable economic opportunities and promoting sustainable development for present and future generations.

Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Commission The Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Commission was constituted as a permanent body 4848 on 15 March 1993 under Article 16(4), read with Article 340 of the Constitution of India, in accordance with the guidelines of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, to advise the Government on the lists of Backward Classes and Most Backward Classes in the State. Sinc e its inception, the Commission has functioned under the chairmanship of a retired Judge of the Hon’ble High Court. At present, the Commission has been reconstituted for a period of three years from 2 nd December 2025 under the Chairmanship of Hon’ble retired Madras High Court Judge Thiru. V. Bharathidasan. The functions of the Commission include s receiving and examining the requests and complaints for inclusion , non -inclusion and over inclusion in the Backward Classes, Most Backward Classes lists, and make recommendations thereon and periodically reviewing the Backward Classes , 49 Most Backward Classes lists in accordance with decisions taken from time to time. The terms of reference of the Commission also include submission of reports on classification and sub -classification of Backward Classes, Most Backward Classes and Denotified Communities based on constitutional provisions and relevant judgements of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, and making recommendations regarding enhanced reservation for minority communities based on social and educational backwardness.

Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Economic Development Corporation (TABCEDCO) The Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Economic Development Corporation (TABCEDCO) was established on 16.11.1981 with the objective of improving the economic condition of Backward Classes, Most Backward Cla sses and Denotified Communities and has been functioning from 22.05.1982. It is a Government undertaking entity registered under the Companies Act, 1956. It 51 provides financial assistance at low rates of interest to individuals and groups belonging to Backward Classes, Most Backward Classes and Denotified Communities to undertake viable small industries, businesses and other economic activities. The authorised Share Capital of the Corporation is Rs.30 crore and its Paid-up Share Capital is Rs.12.27 crore. Th is Corporation functions as the State Channelising Agency of the National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation. Funds for the various loan schemes implemented by the Corporation are borrowed from the National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation against the guarantee of the Government of Tamil Nadu.

Tamil Nadu Narikuravar Welfare Board 135 1 SOCIAL JUSTICE DEPARTMENT POLICY NOTE 2026-27 INTRODUCTION The Adi Dravidar and Tribal Welfare Department was established as a separate department in 1988 by bifurcating it from the Social Welfare Department. The Department was created to formulate and implement focused schemes for the educational, social and economic advancement of Adi Dravidar and Tribal communities, with the objective of improving their overall standard of living.

Details of Educational Scholarship (Rs. per annum) Day Scholar Hosteller 3,500/- (Classes 1 – 10) 8,000/- (Classes 3 – 10) (ii) Girls Incentive Scheme The Girls Incentive Scheme is being implemented for girl children studying in Classes 3 t o 8 , s o a s t o e n c o u r a g e A d i D r a v i d a r a n d Christian Adi Dravidar girl students studying in Government and Government-aided schools to pursue their education without dropping out, and to ensure 100 percent enrolment. The incentive provided to girl students under this scheme is as follows:- (Rs. per annum) Class Amount III to V 500/- VI 1,000/- VII and VIII 1,500/- 76 equivalent occupations who are studying in Classes 1 to 10 in schools.

Lands are acquired either through individual negotiation or the Land Acquisition laws in force, and house site pattas are granted to eligible beneficiaries. Under this scheme, the annual income ceiling for beneficiaries has been fixed at Rs.1,00,000/-. An allocation of Rs.6 crore per annum is provided for this scheme. items.text: 11.DR. AMBEDKAR AWARD In order to eradicate caste distinctions in society and to establish equality, the Dr. Ambedkar Award is presented every year on Thiruvalluvar Day by the Hon'ble Chief Minister to a person belonging to Tamil Nadu who has rendered service for Adi Dravidar and Tribal people. Along with this award, a cheque for a prize amount of Rs.5,00,000/-, a citation and an 8-gram gold medal are presented. From the year 1998 up to the year 2025, the Government of Tamil Nadu has presented the Dr. Ambedkar Award to 28 persons who h a v e r e n d e r e d s e r v i c e f o r A d i D r a v i d a r a n d Tribal people. 4342 Under this scheme, financial assistance of Rs.1,00,000/- each, or the cost of publishing the selected books, whichever is less, is being provided to 11 writers, comprising 10 Adi Dravidar / Tribal / Christian Adi Dravidar writers and 1 writer belonging to a non-Adi Dravidar community. 11.DR. DEVELOPMENT ACTION PLAN FOR THE SCHEDULED CASTE AND THE SCHEDULED TRIBES With the objective of improving the social, economic and educational status of Adi Dravidar and Tribal people, the Tribal Sub-Plan has been implemented from the year 1976-1977 and the Adi Dravidar Sub-Plan from the year 1980-1981. In the fund allocation for the welfare schemes implemented in Government departments, funds are allocated to the extent of 20.01 percent and 1.17 percent respectively, in proportion to the population of Adi Dravidar and Tribal people. On 29.05.2024, the Tamil Nadu Development Action Plan for the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribes Act 20 / 2024 w a s e n a c t e d . T h e p u r p o s e o f t h i s A c t i s t o provide for the preparation, approval, implementation and monitoring of the Development Action Plan for the Scheduled caste and the Scheduled Tribes, for the computation and earmarking of funds in proportion to population, and for undertaking matters connected therewith.

Aandror Velanmai Melanmai Thittam The Aandror Velanmai Melanmai Thittam has been formulated to implement livelihood schemes for Tribal people, in collaboration with governmental and non-governmental voluntary organisations. Its principal objectives are livelihood schemes such as farm / non-farm occupations, improvement in animal husbandry, modern brackish-water fish rearing, and value addition centres relating to Minor Forest Produce 81 (MFP), and these are being implemented in 13 districts. This scheme is implemented through six governmental institutions, such as ICAR-NBFGR (National Bureau of Fish Genetic Resources) and the Tamil Nadu Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, and four non- governmental organisations. • Farm Machinery Hiring Centres 20 Tribal farmers' associations have been formed and farm machinery hiring centres established in the districts of Salem, Tiruvannamalai, Kallakurichi, Nilgiris, Tirupathur, Erode, Namakkal, Dharmapuri, Vellore, Coimbatore, Perambalur and Tiruchirappalli. This comprises a 90% Government subsidy and a 10% contribution from the farmers' association.

Through these centres, modern machineries including tractors, harvesters, seed drills, power tillers, power sprayers and rotavators have been provided, and about 4,700 Tribal farming families are benefiting. This scheme, which increases the cultivated area by shifting from traditional agriculture to modern farm machinery methods, is being implemented with the 8282 o b j e c t i v e o f r e d u c i n g t h e c o s t o f c u l t i v a t i o n b y 30% and doubling the yield. • Ainthinai – Pasumai Pannai Thittam In order to improve the economy of the Tribals residing in the districts of Kallakurichi, Tiruvannamalai, Dharmapuri, Coimbatore, Erode, Krishnagiri, Nilgiris, Namakkal, Tiruvallur, Tiruchirappalli, Cuddalore and Tirupathur, the “Ainthinai Pasumai Pannai Thittam through Tribal Farmers' Associations” is being implemented. This scheme is being implemented for the economic advancement of Tribal people by protecting the traditional agricultural practices of Tribals and, using modern scientific technology, increasing agricultural productivity through the use of heritage seeds and natural fertilisers suited to the natural environment and the nature of the agricultural land. As another component of this scheme, value addition centres and solar-powered millet grinding centres have been established and are functioning through Tribal farmers' associations and Tribal women's self-help groups.

The Corporation was created to effectively implement initiatives such as the education, basic infrastructure and economic development through various projects, including entrepreneurship and skill development, training, maintenance of school and hostel buildings for the welfare of Adi Dravidar and Tribal people. The paid-up capital of the board has been shared by the State a nd Union Government in the ratio of 51:49 since 1980. Laws relating to Industrial Relations These laws provide a framework for conditions of employment, dispute resolution, industrial relations, collective bargaining and structured mechanisms for resolving disputes. They empower workers to form trade unions and negotiate collective agreements with management. Standing Orders establish legally binding rules that clearly define the terms and conditions of employment. 13 1.3.1.1. Resolution of Industrial Disputes Conciliation is an effective dispute resolution process where the Conciliation Officer as neutral third party, assists employers and workers in resolving industrial disputes or conflicts amicably. It is vital for maintaining industrial harmony, preventing work stoppages and ensuring that production continues without any interruption. The Department official portal, https://labour.tn.gov.in, provides online registration, licensing, renewal and other services under various labour enactments and the Legal Metrology laws. This enables employers and establishments to comply with statutory requirements conveniently and transparently. 40 services of this department notified under the Tamil Nadu Information Technology (Electronic Service Delivery) Rules, 2016, have been made available online. These include registration under the 56 56 Tamil Nadu Shops and Establishments Act and the Tamil Nadu Catering Establishments Act, as well as licences for manufacturers, dealers and repairers under the Legal Metrology Act, etc., Faceless and paperless processing, automated workflows, online inspection systems, digitally issued certificates and deemed-approval mechanisms have also been introduced. These reforms enable end-to-end online delivery of services without any need for the applicants to visit departmental offices. 1.6. WELFARE BOARDS AND SOCIAL SECURITY SCHEMES 1.6.1. Tamil Nadu Labour Welfare Board The Tamil Nadu Labour Welfare Board was constituted to implement welfare programmes for workers in the organised 57 sector in the State. The Board extends its services to eligible employees working in factories, plantations, motor transport undertakings, shops, catering establishments and other notified establishments. The Labour Welfare Fund is supported through annual contributions of Rs.20 per employee, Rs.40 per worker from the employer and Rs.20 from the Government. The Board also receives fines imposed by courts and compounding fees collected by the enforcement officers of the Labour Department for violations of labour laws and rules.

The scope of the scheme comprises of the following activities. • Providing medical services to Insured Persons and their family members through ESI dispensaries, ESI hospitals and empanel led hospitals. • Protecting insured persons against financial and social hardships arising from sickness, maternity, employment injury, disablement, death and other contingencies. • Providing outpatient and inpatient treatment, specialist and super-speciality care, medicines, 122 122 diagnostic services, maternity care and other necessary healthcare facilities. • Reimbursement for the treatment of Insured Persons and their family members at private Hospitals other than Tie -up Hospitals in case of emergencies. • Providing cashless treatment to the Insured Persons and their family members through Speciality and Super Speciality private tie -up hospitals under the package rates of the Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS). 3.2. In accordance with Vettri Tamizhagam Vision, special focus is laid on Artificial Intelligence , Machine Learning technologies in training and new trades related to this sector are proposed to be introduced in ITIs to enhance the employability of youth at global level. 164 164 Skill training in ITIs provide students with practical knowledge, technical expertise and industry -relevant skills. In order to improve the relevance in skill learning, ITIs have introduced cluster -based learning, Industry 4.0 labs, job placement cells, digital learning modules, software tools and stronger partnerships with industries. Accordingly, ITIs under the Training Wing of the Department are offering long -term training to youth and preparing them to meet the changing requirements of the industries. Emphasis is also laid on introducing Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality in skill training courses in ITIs. 4.23. Government ITIs are functioning under the leadership of Principals and District Skill Training Offices are headed by the Assistant Directors. The Department implements the following major skill development programmes. • Craftsmen Training Scheme • Industry 4.0 Technology Centres • Apprenticeship Training Scheme • Industrial Schools • Short-term skill training 166 166 4.24. CRAFTSMEN TRAINING SCHEME The Craftsmen Training Scheme is the cornerstone of vocational training in Tamil Nadu. It provides long -term, structured training through Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), equipping youth with industry -ready skills to meet present and future workforce demands. Training under Craftsmen Training Scheme comprises 70% practical training and 30% theoretical learning, ensuring balanced skill acquisition. 4.24.1. Long-Term Skill Training in Government ITIs In Tamil Nadu, 132 Government Industrial Training Institutes impart long - term comprehensive skill training in 70 Engineering and 34 Non -Engineering Trades with the seating capacity of 36,344. 167 Skill Training is imparted in conventional trades such as Welder, Turner, Fitter, Mechanic Motor Vehicle, Plumber and new age trades including Power Electronics, Architectural Assistant, Technician Medical Electronics, Operator Advanced Machine Tools, Fire Technology and Industrial Safety Management. Training is also imparted in Industry 4.0 trades like Advanced CNC, Electric Vehicle, Industrial Robotics, etc. ITI Courses range from 6 months to 2 years with admissions conducted annually in July through centralized online counselling at www.skilltraining.tn.gov.in, following merit and reservation norms.

Most of these ITIs are minority institutions. Government subsidies are extended to these institutes to provide skill training to students hailing from downtrodden society to uplift their livelihood. A sum of Rs.2.75 crore has been provided to these ITIs as maintenance grant for the last year. 4.28. items.text: To support this objective, a short -term skill training programme has been designed for trainees in the Electrician and Wireman trades under CTS from ITIs. The target group includes both final -year trainees and passed-outs, who are equipped with foundational electrical skills and can be readily upskilled for Solar PV installation and maintenance. 197 Implementation is facilitated through convergence with industry partners. A minimum of two days of On -the-Job Training is provided through empaneled vendors, ensuring hands -on practical training. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy and the Rural Electrification Corporation play a key role in coordinating linkages between training institutions and vendors for seamless execution. Assessment of trainees is conducted through a summative evaluation process at the end of the course, covering technical skills, knowledge and professional attitude, as prescribed by the Directorate General of Training (DGT). So far, 867 ITI trainees have been trained under this initiative in the last two years. 197 196 49 Government ITIs have been mapped with 117 nearby Government Higher Secondary Schools. The duration of the short -term courses ranges from 15 to 30 days. 4.41. To support this objective, a short -term skill training programme has been designed for trainees in the Electrician and Wireman trades under CTS from ITIs.

items.text: To support this objective, a short -term skill training programme has been designed for trainees in the Electrician and Wireman trades under CTS from ITIs. The target group includes both final -year trainees and passed-outs, who are equipped with foundational electrical skills and can be readily upskilled for Solar PV installation and maintenance. 197 Implementation is facilitated through convergence with industry partners. A minimum of two days of On -the-Job Training is provided through empaneled vendors, ensuring hands -on practical training. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy and the Rural Electrification Corporation play a key role in coordinating linkages between training institutions and vendors for seamless execution. Assessment of trainees is conducted through a summative evaluation process at the end of the course, covering technical skills, knowledge and professional attitude, as prescribed by the Directorate General of Training (DGT). Proposed as a hub -and-spoke model, it aims to introduce demand -driven, industry-aligned courses, revamp existing trades, and establish Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) with anchor industry partners for outcome -based training. The scheme enhances capacity, fosters innovation, and ensures that training outputs remain closely aligned with industry requirements.

items.text: 4.47. INSTITUTE MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE IN GOVERNMENT ITIS Institute Management Committees (IMCs) play a crucial role in strengthening the link between vocational training and industry requirements. They ensure that Government ITIs remain responsive to the dynamic labour market by involving industry representatives directly in planning, managing and upgrading training activities. 206 206 This collaboration helps to bridge the gap between classroom learning and workplace skills, making trainees more employable. IMCs provide autonomy to ITIs in areas such as curriculum enrichment, infrastructure modernization and resource mobilization. By including industry partners as chairpersons, IMCs ensure that, training programmes are aligned with current technologies and practices. They also facilitate internships, apprenticeships and placement opportunities, thereby enhancing the employability of students. In Tamil Nadu, IMCs have been constituted in 100 Government ITIs, which has enabled ITIs to introduce new trades and modernize workshops in collaboration with industry. 207 4.48. Through Memorandum of Understanding (MoUs), industries provide shop -floor exposure, internships, guest lectures and participation in Institute Management Committees. Ltd., Grey Sim Learning Foundations, Schneider Electric, etc., exemplify this collaborative approach. Introduction The Government of Tamil Nadu, under the leadership of the Hon'ble Chief Minister, has formulated the "Vetri Tamizhagam – Vision Document" to provide a strategic direction for the State's long -term development. The schemes outlined under this Vision Document are intended to promote balanced socio-economic development 2 2 across the State and to ensure that the benefits of development reach all sections of society. The schemes / programmes envisaged in the Vision Document are structured to benefit every citizen with a special focus on the welfare of women, farmers, fisherme n, marginalized communities and youth of Tamil Nadu. It also aims at upholding Tamil identity and pride while insisting on providing dignified living for the people of the State.
